items.title: cold-store: atlas /dump download cut mid-transfer (curl 18) on every attempt; endpoint ignores Range so no resume is possible
items.body:
## Problem

The `atlas` Turso export can now fail one stage earlier than #12000's rebuild defect: the `/dump` download itself is cut mid-transfer, and the endpoint offers no way to resume.

First-hand evidence, 2026-11-23 01:57–02:23 CST (a standalone run of the atlas leg of `export-turso.sh` — token mint, `/dump` download, filters, rebuild — filing nothing):

- 4 download attempts (the script's initial try + `--retry 3 --retry-all-errors`): **all four ended `curl: (18) transfer closed with outstanding read data remaining`**, at varying offsets (the first reached ~1.28 GB; later attempts were cut far earlier).
- Range probe straight after: the endpoint answers a `Range:` request with **HTTP 200 and no `Content-Range`** — it ignores the header and streams from the start, so `curl -C -` resume cannot work against it.
- Throughput in the probe's last windows was ~3–6 KB/s (76–190 KB per 30 s), far below the ~3 MB/s the same download started at — the stream is being starved or stalled, then closed.

Circumstantial match: the 2026-11-22 nightly filed 50 databases (transfer ledger, 09:12–09:44 UTC) but **no atlas**, and `cold-store-nightly.service` exited FAILURE at 04:20 CST. Atlas is exported last, so a download that keeps getting cut fits — but it cannot be confirmed after the fact, because **no output from the unit survives**: `journalctl --user -u cold-store-nightly.service` returns no entries at all.

## Relation to #12000

Distinct stage. #12000's defect (rebuild dying on a duplicated `chunk_id` from a repeated table in the dump) is fixed — dedupe/vector-index filters on main — and its acceptance was met on 2026-11-19 and 2026-11-21 (atlas filed, 3,581,679,110 bytes gzipped each time; filing only happens after `integrity_check = ok` and the user-table check pass). This issue is the download stage that now fails first on bad nights.

## Ask

1. **Durable nightly output:** the nightly unit's per-step outcome and ERROR lines must survive the run (a log file under the cold-store home, or equivalent), so the next failure names its stage without a live probe.
2. **A download strategy that survives a cut, non-resumable stream:** e.g. spread the largest database's whole-download retries across the run's existing deadline budget instead of four attempts inside a few minutes, so a bad window can pass; or an alternate export path for `atlas`. Restarting a 10+ GB stream from zero on every attempt is the current shape and it is not working on bad nights.
3. **Acceptance:** three consecutive nightly runs file an `atlas` export, or one files it on a night when a probe shows the stream being cut.

Found by Lane LR while reconciling #12000.

items.body:
## PM push unification — one registry, one sender, the Android app as a first-class endpoint

**Drew's order (2026-11-23):** "start a lane now to unify push between the like 2 pm stack locations and the pm stack android app."

**Full design of record:** dated doc record `doc/2026-11-24T04-45-43Z_design_pm-push-unification/` (doc-only PR linked below when landed). This body is the faithful summary; the doc record governs.

### Premise check — the landscape is worse than "two locations" (verified 2026-11-23, code + live stores)

There are **four Web Push senders, three subscription stores (+ one mirror), three VAPID keypairs, and two incompatible class/preference models**:

| Location | Store (live count) | Classes | Sender / keys | Surfaces |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Aggregator** (laptop, `pm-stack/aggregator`) | Turso `alerts.push_subscriptions` — **0** (2026-11-23, #14048); sends ledger `alerts.notification_sends` — 271 rows, none after 2026-11-17, 269/269 undated per the roll-up (#14061) | 8 toggleable: `incident`, `needs-drew`, `quota-wall`, `quota-near-wall`, `section-risk`, `stack-health`, `blocked-age`, `prompt` (+ `digest` as a delivery shape) | `web-push` library; VAPID pair **A** (public key in code, private in Bitwarden by name) | `/alerts`, `/alerts/preferences`, `/notifications` at the tailnet URL |
| **Console origin** (laptop, `pm-stack/console` `src/server.ts`) | File store `~/.local/state/pm-console/push.json` — **0** (live count tonight) | 4: `replies`, `needs`, `questions`, `trouble` — toggled by a **store-global** off-list, not per subscription | Hand-rolled RFC 8291/8292 (`src/push.ts`); VAPID pair **B** in the store file | The console site at its origin; `GET /push` delivery status |
| **Console edge** (Cloudflare, `pm-stack/console/edge`) | KV store (`kvStore(kv, "push")`) — **count not readable from the laptop**; no census route exists | Same 4 (same code) | Same hand-rolled sender, VAPID pair **C** held in the KV store document | `pm.security.cab` — the live site the Android app wraps |
| **Notify-relay** (Cloudflare DO, `pm-stack/notify-relay`, #8569) | Mirror of the aggregator's full set (snapshot POST on change, seq-ordered) | Sends only `stack.silent` + recovered, riding `incident` | Own `push.ts`, reusing pair **A** (private key as a Worker secret) | `GET /status` only |

**The Android app** (`pm-stack/console/android`, package `today.developing.pmconsole`) is a Trusted Web Activity over the console site: it has **no push channel of its own** — the *console's* Web Push arrives as the app's notifications. Its widget polls a summary every ~30 min on a separate read-only device token (`console/src/devices.ts`), an identity registry unrelated to push subscriptions.

**Consequences, plainly:**
- The app Drew actually uses can only ever receive the console's 4 classes. The answerable `needs-drew` pushes (the ones #14043's write-back serves), the quota family, `section-risk`, `stack-health`, `blocked-age`, `prompt` can only reach an aggregator browser subscription — of which there are currently **zero**.
- #14048 ("delivery dark") and #14061 ("pushes do reach Drew's phone") are **both true — of different stacks**.
- Nobody can answer "how many live push endpoints exist?" — the edge KV store has no census route, and the other two stores are both empty.
- Class models diverge: the aggregator's preferences are per-subscription (class map + quiet hours); the console's are store-global. Twelve distinct class ids exist across the stacks with near-miss overlaps (`needs` vs `needs-drew`, `trouble` vs `incident`/`stack-health`).
- #14061's blindness is structural: `AlertsStore.logSend`'s insert names **no timestamp column** — the send time rides on a column default in a SQL-translated store, and the roll-up's parser rejects what the live rows carry (269/269 excluded).

### The design (summary — doc record governs)

1. **One registry.** `push_endpoints` + per-endpoint preference rows in the fleet-platform Turso store — hosted, already the aggregator's store, and reachable from the console edge over HTTPS (the same store family the edge already uses for decision sets). An endpoint row names its **transport** (`webpush`), its **client** (`browser` | `android-app`), an optional link to the console device registry, label, user agent, created/last-seen, gone count. The Android app's TWA-held subscription registers as an endpoint in its own right — named, countable, preference-bearing as the app — and the transport column is where a future native (FCM) transport lands without redesign.
2. **One sender.** A single send service owning VAPID pair **A**; every producer submits candidates to it. The aggregator engine and the console Notifier both become producers into the one candidate path (dedupe/cooldown/fingerprint/quiet-hours machinery is the aggregator's, reused). The notify-relay keeps pair A and its mirror as the designed exception — a sender of last resort whose whole purpose is the primary being down. Console origin + edge `Push` instances retire as senders; pairs B and C retire with them.
3. **One class taxonomy.** The union of the 12 ids, each with exactly one producer of record. `needs` (console census-diff: new needs-me items) and `needs-drew` (answerable attention-tier questions) stay **distinct ids with distinct labels** in v1 — merging them is a product decision flagged below, not an engineering default. `stack.silent` remains a payload variant of `incident` at the relay. `digest` remains a delivery shape, never a class.
4. **One preference model.** Per-endpoint class map + quiet hours (the aggregator's model — the richer one). The console's store-global off-list migrates onto its endpoints' maps. One preferences surface, served from the console (pm.security.cab — where Drew and the app live), backed by the registry; the aggregator's `/alerts/preferences` keeps working during migration, then redirects there.
5. **Event-driven at detection.** Producers emit at their detection points (broker/watchdog raises, quota snapshot transitions, console state-doc diffs, relay alarm) into the candidate intake — per Drew's standing requirement, the stack pushes itself; no new polling loops are introduced.
6. **Answerable pushes unchanged.** The `needs-drew` payload contract (ledger id + options + per-question answer landing) is preserved exactly, and must work identically when the endpoint is the app (the TWA already intercepts pm.security.cab links). Answer *application* remains #14043's territory; edge answer intake (#13469) composes unchanged.
7. **Delivery observability by construction.** One sends ledger in the registry store: one row per attempt, `sent_at` stamped **by the writer** (ISO-8601 UTC, schema-required — never a column default again), endpoint id, class, object ref, outcome incl. push-service status, `acted_on_at` via the existing Ack transition. Two designed-in alarms: **undated-row alarm** (any row the roll-up cannot date is a data defect that pages — this subsumes #14061's alarm ask for the unified ledger; #14061 remains the vehicle for the legacy ledger's repair/backfill) and the **zero-endpoint sentinel** (#14048's detection ask): zero live endpoints while undelivered incidents exist — or no successful send in N days with incidents open — raises a stack-health incident on a **non-push** surface, because a push about no-push is a dead letter by definition. A census read (endpoints by transport/client + last successful send) is exposed on both stacks' status surfaces: one answer to "how many live endpoints?"

### Migration

- Aggregator subscriptions: none live — nothing to move; its schema shape seeds the registry.
- Console edge subscriptions **cannot be re-keyed**: a Web Push subscription is bound to the application-server key used at subscribe time, so pair-C subscriptions cannot be carried to pair A as rows. Migration is a **re-subscription**: the console site/app detects the sender-key change via its existing endpoint-mark mechanism (built for exactly this — "so the app can tell that this sender has lost it") and re-subscribes under pair A into the registry. The KV store freezes read-only for one release, then drops. Console origin store: empty — retired outright.
- Relay mirror source switches from the aggregator store to the registry (same snapshot protocol, same secret by name).
- Legacy sends ledger stays as-is under #14061; the unified ledger starts at cutover and the `/notifications` roll-up reads it from then on.

### Boundaries

Not this design's: #14043 (answer write-back — untouched), #13469 (edge answer intake — composes), #8570 (service consolidation — the sender's natural eventual home, not a prerequisite), native FCM/APNs transport (v2 option the registry's transport column reserves), #14061's legacy-ledger backfill (linked, not duplicated).

### Build-slice map (ordered; **not packetised** — reason below)

- **S1 — Registry + aggregator adoption.** Unified endpoint/preference tables in fleet-platform Turso; `AlertsStore` reads/writes them; `/alerts/preferences` unchanged externally. Proof: aggregator notification test suite + a live subscribe → test-send on the laptop.
- **S2 — Unified sends ledger + observability.** Writer-stamped `sent_at`; roll-up on the unified ledger; undated-row alarm; zero-endpoint sentinel wired into stack-health (lands #14048's detection ask); census read. Needs S1.
- **S3 — Sender consolidation.** Console Notifier becomes a producer to the one sender (pair A); console origin `Push` retires. Proof: the 4 console classes delivered by the unified sender to a browser endpoint. Needs S1.
- **S4 — Edge cutover + app endpoint.** Edge `Push` retires as sender; subscribe path writes the registry with client + device link; endpoint-mark-driven re-subscription under pair A; the one preferences surface on pm.security.cab; `/alerts/preferences` redirect. Needs S3.
- **S5 — Relay re-point + close-out.** Mirror source = registry; legacy stores frozen/dropped; closure evidence for #14048/#14061 (census ≥ 1 live endpoint per class path; a week of dated sends). Needs S4.

**Why no packet yet:** two seams must be settled on this record before any slice is specified exactly — (i) the `needs`/`needs-drew` taxonomy call is Drew-facing (it changes what his toggles say) and is posed here for his word; (ii) S4's re-subscription slice can only be specified against the endpoint-mark flow's behaviour in the *shipped* app build, which the S3/S4 builder must verify live first. S1/S2 are close to specifiable and packetise on this design's acceptance — the #14043 pattern (design of record first, build slices from it).

### Open questions for Drew

1. Class taxonomy: keep `needs` and `needs-drew` as separate toggles (recommended — different promises: "new items need your hands" vs "a question only you can answer"), or merge into one "Needs you" class?
2. Preferences surface home: console (pm.security.cab) as the one surface, aggregator page redirecting — as designed — or the reverse?

— Lane PUSH-UNIFY, 2026-11-24. Progress + records on this issue at each boundary.

items.body:
## Build: fleet file transfer — get / put / copy verbs (SCP-class, any-to-any)

Origin: Drew, 2026-11-14 — "we should add it as its own build item." This is the
implementation issue for the design in #5759 (`fleet proxy get`/`put` over the
agent channel), with the read-path alternative in #5757 §3 and Drew's
2026-11-14 requirements folded in. Epic: #5412. Daemon: #5343.

### Verified current state (2026-11-14)

- No file-transfer verb exists anywhere in the fleet binary. Domains:
  queue, serve, proxy, dispatch, dispatch-test, secrets, gh, search,
  laptop-agent. Everything carried today is commands and small JSON.
- The laptop-agent daemon's routes are exec + jobs only; every body is JSON.
  Files cross today only as (a) base64 inside exec calls (manual, ~33% size
  tax, ~1 MiB/stream practical cap, no resume), (b) stdin pushes over the
  real-SSH fallback (`fetch-charge-inputs.py`, `atlas-backup.py` — the two
  scripts #5759 names as waiting on this channel), or (c) out-of-band staging
  (the rclone-crypt → R2 path built for the sandbox-home backup move,
  hatch-personal#50 — proven both directions 2026-11-14, but it is a backup
  pipeline, not a general verb).
- The "more performant HTTP version" in Drew's memory is the agent's *exec*
  transport (commands over HTTP through pooled CONNECT tunnels) — it has
  never carried files. Recorded already on #5759 (2026-11-04).

### Requirements (Drew, 2026-11-14)

1. **At least SCP-capable.** `fleet get`, `fleet put`, and a `fleet copy`
   that takes SCP-style addressing on BOTH sides:
   `fleet copy sandbox:/home/hatch/test.txt laptop:/home/user/test2.txt`.
   Either side may be a remote; a bare path means the local host.
2. **The target is a parameter, never a hardcoded "the laptop."** Every
   connect-family verb takes an explicit remote/endpoint name
   (`--remote NAME` or the `host:` prefix). Today everything silently
   defaults to the one laptop; the addressing must generalize to
   laptop1/laptop2/pool members without a redesign. (Coordinator/pool
   routing — a lookup that picks the endpoint by command, load, or
   stickiness — is future work; the addressing must not preclude it.)
3. **Integrity end-to-end.** Hash-verified transfer (the #5759
   begin/write/commit protocol already specifies sha256 + deterministic
   temp names + atomic commit — implement that; the #5757 §3 raw
   byte-range GET is the candidate read path if profiling wants it).
4. **Resumable + clean.** An interrupted transfer resumes the same temp
   file instead of restarting; partial transfers are never visible at the
   destination path; abandoned temps are swept.
5. **Delegated (direct-path) copy is designed in from the start.** When
   source and destination can reach each other directly, the controller
   should be able to authorize and instruct the copy instead of relaying
   every byte through itself: the source validates the instruction and
   pushes/pulls directly. The naive relay path is the fallback and may
   ship first — but if the delegated path is not in v1, it MUST be split
   out as its own follow-on issue before this one closes (Drew: "it is
   not a question of whether it's a thing — that should be a thing").
6. **Performance close-out.** Report measured throughput for a 100 MiB
   file sandbox↔laptop against: base64-over-exec (today), scp over the
   proxy SSH path, and the new verb. The bar: decisively beat base64-exec,
   at least match scp.

### Acceptance

- [ ] 100 MiB file sandbox→laptop and laptop→sandbox, sha256-identical.
- [ ] Transfer killed mid-flight resumes and completes; destination path
      never shows partial content.
- [ ] `fleet copy laptop:/path sandbox:/path` and the reverse both work
      with explicit host addressing.
- [ ] The two waiting scripts (`fetch-charge-inputs.py`,
      `atlas-backup.py`) migrated off SSH-stdin pushes, or a recorded
      reason they stay.
- [ ] Delegated copy: working, OR follow-on issue filed and linked here.
- [ ] Throughput numbers posted in the close-out comment.

Related: #5759 (design), #5757 (perf census), #5697 (`fleet proxy ssh`),
#5972 (fallback connection mode), #5345 / #1794 (the ID project's own
server-to-server transfer designs — coordinate so the fleet verb and the
ID protocol do not grow into two incompatible answers).

items.body:
## Status quo (verified 2026-10-28)

The flake's nixos/services/ defines cloudflared, flatpak, id-mail, and pm-stack (aggregator, projector, git-sync, projector-reconcile). Four PM-stack servers are NOT in the flake at all (zero mentions in nixos/ or home/): they run as hand-made units/containers on the laptop, are not enabled as boot services, and would not come back on their own after a reboot:

- **Grist** (:8484) — roadmap table + registers; its own document storage.
- **Kaneo** (:5173) — task board; Postgres-backed (see code#1514: its database has no backup routine, docker volume is the only copy).
- **Pad** (:7777) — notes; token expires 2027-01-22.
- **ready-for-agent** (:6056) — agent intake endpoint.

## What to build

- One nixos/services module per server (or one pm-apps module) in this flake, following the pm-stack module's shape: service runs from the primary checkout or a pinned package, state under ~/.local/state/<name>/ (or the server's existing data home — do NOT orphan Kaneo's Postgres data or Grist's docs; migrate or bind the existing data in place).
- Enabled at switch like the rest of the fleet; hand units retired in the same change that proves the NixOS unit serves.
- Backup coverage for each server's data lands with or before the move (code#1514, code#1516).

## Acceptance

- After a NixOS switch, all four answer on their ports with their existing data intact.
- A laptop reboot brings all four back with no hand step.
- The hand-made units/containers are removed; 'systemctl --user is-enabled' is no longer the thing standing between the stack and a reboot.

Raised by Drew 2026-10-28 ('what is status for implementing nixos services for all the servers?'). Related: code#1199 (projector deploy — done interim, NixOS at the switch), code#1514, code#1516, code#1744 (shared-schema direction for these servers' data).

## Acceptance criteria

- Each of Grist (:8484), Kaneo (:5173), Pad (:7777), and ready-for-agent (:6056) is defined as a NixOS/flake service in this repo, following the pm-stack module shape, with state under `~/.local/state/<name>/` or its existing data home bound/migrated in place — Kaneo's Postgres data and Grist's documents are not orphaned.
- After a NixOS switch, all four servers answer on their existing ports with their existing data intact.
- A laptop reboot brings all four back with no hand step.
- The hand-made units/containers are retired in the same change that proves the NixOS units serve.
- Backup coverage for each server's data lands with or before the move (see #1514, #1516).

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

items.body:
## Design + build: `fleet connect` — explicit transport selection, sessions, and drop semantics

Origin: Drew's questions, 2026-11-14. Epic: #5412. Builds on #5343
(laptop-agent), #5697 (`fleet proxy ssh`), #5972 (fallback connection
mode), and the session semantics of the file-transfer build (sibling
issue filed the same day).

### Verified current state (2026-11-14) — what Drew asked to confirm

Three ways to reach the laptop exist today, chosen by *which tool you
invoke*, not by a flag:

1. **Agent exec** (`laptop-agent.py`, the day-to-day path; the Rust
   `fleet laptop-agent` domain is still a registry stub — exit 69,
   "implementation lands in a later step of epic #5412"). Commands run
   as argv directly on the laptop, **no shell** unless `--shell` is
   passed (then a login `bash -lc`). Environment is the daemon's
   systemd-user-service environment (plus the login profile under
   `--shell`) — nothing from the caller's environment crosses. **There
   is no stdin channel at all**: interactive input during a run is
   impossible on this path, which is exactly why stdin-carrying shapes
   fall back to SSH. Transport is HTTP over pooled CONNECT tunnels
   through the session proxy (warm call ~0.39–0.45 s; cold CONNECT
   ~1.8 s — all traffic hairpins the NYC DERP relay).
2. **Detached agent jobs** (`run` / `poll` / `kill` / `jobs` on the same
   daemon). Jobs persist server-side: spool files under
   `~/.local/state/laptop-agent/jobs/` on the laptop survive client
   death, disconnection, and sandbox restarts; `poll` resumes output by
   byte offset (client offsets in `~/.cache/laptop-agent/`). This is
   the one place a session/resume model already exists.
3. **Real SSH** (`laptop-ssh-real.sh`, or `fleet proxy ssh` in the
   binary since the 2026-11-11 refresh): full SSH over an HTTP CONNECT
   ProxyCommand, connection-multiplexed (ControlMaster, ControlPersist
   600 s; sshd MaxStartups raised to 200 after the 2026-10-25 root
   cause). Real shells, real PTY, real stdin/stdout/stderr streaming,
   port forwards, the laptop login environment. Drew's belief is
   correct: this is the only path with true interactive sessions today.
   The shim (`laptop-ssh.sh`) auto-routes: exec-shaped calls go to the
   agent; interactive / forwards / stdin-carrying calls go to real SSH.

Drop semantics today, per path:

- Agent **exec**: a client disconnect deliberately *reaps* the remote
  command (own process group, TERM→KILL; fixed 2026-11-10, #5343) —
  nothing is buffered for later pickup; a hiccup loses the run.
- Agent **jobs**: the job keeps running and its output spools to disk;
  reconnect and `poll` from the last offset. Buffer limit is effectively
  disk; no replay cap is specified.
- **SSH**: a drop kills nothing server-side (sshd owns the process) but
  there is no output replay — whatever printed while you were gone is
  gone unless the program itself logged it. `timeout` on the SSH path
  bounds only the local wait.
- The sandbox has **no inbound path at all**: no SSH in, no HTTP in.
  Every connection is initiated from the sandbox side or rendezvoused
  through the session proxy / brokers. (Confirmed 2026-11-14.)

### What to design and build

1. **One surface, explicit method.** `fleet connect` wraps all three
   paths with `--method exec|ssh|job|auto`. `auto` codifies the shim's
   current heuristics (stdin data or PTY or forwards → ssh; detached →
   job; else exec). Callers can always force a method — Drew: "is there
   a way to actually flag and choose the SSH connection method versus
   the other?"
2. **A session model across paths.** Generalize the daemon's job spool
   into named connect sessions: `fleet connect session <id>` attaches
   (replays output from offset, like `poll` does today), `fleet
   connect sessions` lists live/recent sessions with metadata (owning
   context id — see the context-propagation design filed the same day —
   command, host, started, state, bytes buffered). Define per-path
   buffering limits and what happens at the cap. Exec-path sessions
   should gain the job path's survive-the-client property *without*
   losing the 2026-11-10 guarantee that an abandoned run does not
   orphan forever: a bounded grace window, then reap.
3. **Stdin decision.** Either the daemon grows a stdin channel (making
   exec interactive-capable), or the routing rule "stdin ⇒ SSH" is
   made permanent and documented as the contract. Pick one on evidence;
   today it is an accident of implementation.
4. **tmux: settle it in writing.** For the SSH path, tmux on the laptop
   IS the attach/detach answer (SSH carries the terminal — there is no
   HTTP attach method and none is needed). For the agent path, jobs +
   spool already cover it. Decide whether a managed tmux pattern
   (named sessions per context id, listable, swept when stale) is
   documented, tooled, or deliberately left manual — and make sure
   anything started under tmux is cleaned up. On the sandbox, Muse's
   own exec sessions already provide the equivalent; do not build a
   second one.
5. **Inbound-less hosts (future, recorded — not ruled out, not a
   priority).** A queue task that instructs a host to open a *reverse*
   connection to a named endpoint, after which that endpoint can drive
   the host's environment. Design space only in this issue; spin out if
   it ever becomes real.
6. **Direct node-to-node (future shape).** Nodes with full network
   access may later SSH directly with per-node client certificates
   under a shared CA, every connection logged under the cert identity,
   with the proxy/coordinator pool as the universal fallback (routing
   by command, load, or session stickiness). The sandbox's network
   idiosyncrasies must keep working automatically underneath all of
   this — the fallback path is the compatibility floor, not a legacy
   mode.

### Acceptance (design phase)

- [ ] Decision record covering items 1–4 with the measured numbers
      (warm/cold per path, batch behaviour, throughput) in one table.
- [ ] Build issues split out for: the `fleet connect` surface, the
      session list/attach surface, and the stdin decision's winner.

labels.name: effort/l

items.body:
# Phase 2 — shared primary + session sweep + grants (global reads, CAS conflicts, supported auth)

- Parent issue: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/10359 (items 2/4/5: central store, sweep survival, five-agent workload).
- Parent design: [reviewed decision record](https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/5ac3ddcec60017b05b655b8fe665b06c61369ec3/doc/2026-11-23T12-45-00Z_design_fleet_kv/2026-11-23T12-45-00Z_design_fleet_kv.md) (§1 hybrid central D014, §4 sweep, §5 CAS, §6 five-agent topology D008, §9 auth D011). Stable decision IDs: D003, D004, D005, D006, D007, D008, D011, D014 (D002 reversed/superseded — do not implement row-scopes-only).
- Prerequisite: design PR https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13294 must merge before this phase starts. Depends on: Phase 1 https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13314 (local verbs + full-identity overlay + durable outbox); its implementation PR must be merged before Phase 2 implementation begins.
- Scope: shared Turso primary over the queue-style libSQL HTTP pipeline at configurable `FLEET_KV_URL` (no hardcoded or fake deployed hostname); proposed migrations/handler paths (no code in this issue): `pkgs/fleet/crates/fleet-kv/migrations/` for `kv_namespaces`, `kv_heads`, `kv_versions`, `kv_conflicts`, `idem_receipts`, `kv_grants`, and pipeline handlers beside the existing queue HTTP handlers. Central key derivation per write/read: from the explicitly selected scope — the shared `scope_id` of the namespace for authorized agents, or the private `scope_id` of the owning `(user, context)` — resolved via `kv_namespaces` + `kv_grants`; no implicit extra fallback scope exists.
- Scope: shared Turso primary over the queue-style libSQL HTTP pipeline; central key `(scope_id, registry_id, namespace, key)` with one shared scope per shared namespace (shared-scope tombstones affect all shared readers; private scopes separate); `kv_namespaces` with designation-only `global_flag`; `kv_grants` with explicit-grant group DBs under fail-closed admission/provisioning policy (no default per-session proliferation; group DBs inline-only — no blob refs, ceiling checked before any group-DB write, blob-needing group writes refuse with `blob_requires_shared_primary`); `--global` now serves central (authoritative bypass); local-first reads (ordinary cache ≤ 1 s; miss/expiry refreshes or typed `unavailable`/`stale`, `--allow-stale` opt-in with age; overlay reads immediate offline) with local-override + merged `list`; durable sweep keyed `(owner_user_id, context_id, session_id)` via outbox + per-key CAS (≤ 5 attempts, jittered exp backoff capped at 1 s), receipts keyed `(authenticated_writer, host_incarnation_UUID, outbox_UUID)` + immutable fingerprint; tombstones sweep through CAS; five-agent rule (single-writer-per-key CAS; KV CAS is not a queue lease — no leases/expiry/steal); 15-minute archive checkpoint TARGET (unbounded loss when offline/unarchived; archive carries inline payloads only up to the effective threshold — no Phase 3 upload here). Auth: RP/agent JWT or route-scoped service token to the trusted endpoint; secrets-broker fetch path is not request auth; per-user Turso data-plane tokens refused (`data_plane_credential_refused`). v1 operational integration ships here: migrations, credential wiring, grant-policy implementation, backup/restore runbook, health probes.

## Acceptance

1. `--global get/set` round-trips against central; plain `get` merges local + central with stated origin marks and never silently hides the shadowed row; `--global` bypasses the 1 s cache.
2. Sweep: session dirty set merges idempotently (re-run safe; retransmit with same key+fingerprint returns the stored result); two sessions racing one key produce one winner + one typed `conflict {expected, actual}` with both versions retrievable — never silent last-writer-wins, never Turso Sync last-push-wins; rebase after conflict is a new intent/new id, never silent overwrite. CAS-before-ack order: receipt written atomically with CAS, ack after; crash between CAS and ack replays the recorded result, never a spurious new conflict.
3. Archive carries inline payloads only (≤ effective threshold) via the archive owner command `fleet kv backup` (equivalently `fleet kv sync --archive` mode) plus the 15-minute online-checkpoint-target sweeper; over-threshold local-working bytes are reported `protection_unavailable_needs_phase3`, never uploaded — no blob upload exists before Phase 3. Over-ceiling bytes addressed to central before Phase 3 land typed `pending_needs_phase3` (queued intent, not a row), never silently buffered inline. Crash before ack re-sweeps fully.
4. Grants: a group DB exists iff a `kv_grants` row authorizes it; unknown group/namespace refuses fail-closed; with no grant, everything lands on the shared primary. No per-session DB is provisioned by default. Group DBs accept inline bytes only: over-ceiling bytes addressed to a group scope refuse with `blob_requires_shared_primary` (shared-primary placement required, no auto-move), so no unrestricted write bypasses the ceiling.
5. Data-plane credential presented to the endpoint is refused with the typed rule, not an incidental signature failure; central access reuses the hosted RP/agent JWT or route-scoped service token path only.
6. Load probe (REQUIRED, correctness-only fixture — not a latency/perf promise, and no billing claim): five writers × ~1–10 keys/min on a ~10k-key namespace all converge; `list` polling observes at most the documented 1 s staleness.
7. Done check from repository root: `cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml -p fleet-kv central` runs the proposed `central_*` model/property/integration suite with a nonzero test count. It must include the five-agent fixture, scope isolation, clear-versus-sweep, same-ID/different-body refusal, duplicate delivery, archive restore, and expired-cache refusal. Also run `cargo test --manifest-path pkgs/fleet/Cargo.toml -p fleet-kv` to preserve Phase 1 behavior. A zero-match filter is failure, not evidence.

## Oracles

- Property: CAS linearity — concurrent same-key writers serialize; the central head always equals one writer's full intent, never a blend; losers get typed conflicts. (PBT over concurrent CAS attempts.)
- Property: sweep idempotence — sweeping the same outbox twice changes central once. (PBT over duplicate deliveries.)
- Property: tombstone sweep convergence — delete-vs-write races resolve to a retrievable conflict or a tombstoned head, never resurrection-by-replay.
- Model: central head machine (version, parent_version, writer) against a sequential CAS oracle; sweep as an outbox-draining refinement of it.

items.title: id(backup): replayed uploads can recreate a backup after account-deletion purge

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

items.body:
## Evidence

Verified on `origin/main` `d7ad9d05efcf48d5a75b851a12e6476cb4776dab` by tracing `pkgs/id/src/backup.rs`:

- `BackupStore::delete` records a tombstone, and `upload` rejects an upload whose epoch is at or below the tombstone's `final_epoch` (`backup.rs:574-580`). The existing deletion test replays the exact original signed upload before purge and gets `Tombstoned` (`backup.rs:1212-1218`).
- `purge_tombstone` is documented as account-deletion cleanup and removes the deleted entry (`backup.rs:727-738`), discarding the only stored final epoch.
- After purge, the same authenticated upload reaches `upload`'s `None` case (`backup.rs:612-628`), which creates a live record without checking a retained epoch or revocation marker. An old, valid signature can therefore recreate the backup after deletion.
- The deletion test checks `NotFound` after purge, but does not replay the old upload afterward (`backup.rs:1224-1226`).

This is source-trace evidence, not a runtime endpoint reproduction. I found no non-test `BackupStore` callsite under `pkgs/id/src`, so this is a store-contract integrity gap; this issue does not claim a currently reachable production endpoint. The larger backup design issue #5033 and implementation issue #7360 do not track this post-purge replay case. All-state issue searches for `purge_tombstone`, replayed/purged backup uploads, and backup resurrection found no exact issue. The open PR #9020 changes restore device binding in the same module, but does not implement this behavior.

## Why it matters

If `purge_tombstone` is the account-deletion boundary, forgetting the tombstone also forgets the anti-replay floor. A previously captured or delayed signed upload can recreate data that the purge was intended to remove.

## Acceptance criteria

- Add a regression that deletes and purges a backup, then replays the exact pre-delete envelope and signature; assert the backup is not recreated.
- Define the post-purge lifecycle rule and enforce it: retain an epoch/revocation marker, or require an authoritative account/key-generation revocation check before accepting uploads for an empty store.
- Keep legitimate backup creation for a new, explicitly authorized identity generation covered by a positive control.

items.body:
Parent design mill: https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/10389

# Design mill pass 4: MCP everywhere — fleet MCP via mcpx, namespaces, fan-out, remote graph

Part of the fleet-surface design mill (Drew, 2026-11-14). Parent issue cross-links all passes.

## The convergence rule

The "connect to all the same things" machinery has already been built three times (MCP, fleet, ID). Do not build a fourth copy. Fleet's MCP should run THROUGH mcpx: fleet starts/connects mcpx, registers fleet's own interface on mcpx's side (an alternate port/socket, a remote URL, or disabled if unwanted; namespaced `fleet`, or `fleet.<hostname>`, `fleet.<hostname>.1`, … on collision), and fleet's conventional MCP endpoint forwards to it. Through mcpx, fleet's MCP gains exec/TypeScript code mode over merged namespaces: local MCP servers, remote GitHub/Cloudflare MCP, iroh-exposed MCP servers via ID's MCP (including passing code-mode scripts into those interfaces, which may themselves reach further mcpx servers).

## Fleet remotes (core functionality, not just MCP)

Fleet needs dynamic connect/disconnect to other fleet instances and remote machines inside its core commands:

- Named remotes with friendly aliases; auth and secrets are managed by the connection as its own unit.
- Every subcommand available locally is available across remotes; admin commands to connect, disconnect, list connections, and inspect each connection's metadata, details, and stats.
- **Fan-out helpers**: `map` (run on each, stream results back as they arrive), collect-all (return when all done), write results to a file; `any`/`some` (first success wins); `first` (like map but any failure cancels). jq-style projection built in (e.g. "just give me the name/path/key from all results into a list"), results piped into shell commands as they stream, tee'd to a file.
- **Tree walking + promotion**: children are only started after the parent succeeds; walking descends secondary connections. A secondary connection can be promoted to the root level where permitted (connected A→B, B→C and B→D: C may refuse promotion while D allows it; the root then exposes B, D, B.C, B.D). Metadata travels with results: depth from the original caller, path taken.
- Example shape Drew gave: `fleet kv get <key>` across all remotes, returning only the failures.

## ID's MCP server

- ID needs an MCP server: the standard ID commands as tools (list/search/get/put blobs, namespaces), plus tooling for common world-app shapes (chat as the worked example).
- App inspection: get an app by ID, hash, or common namespace — name, details, server-side stats, links to comments/reviews, versions, releases, previous versions (a graph on the backend). List a world's standard commands; list its MCP commands if it provides them; hints for common shapes/schemas/tools.
- Dynamic attach: load all of a world's tools into the ID MCP session, or attach the world — the tool set updates live when the world adds/removes tools or changes arguments.
- World apps may offer code mode (a roc script, or another format, inside the app's own server code, with access to a series of app commands and conditionals). ID also has its own code mode: an MCP command running a script against the ID server's platform, as client or as admin — distinct from an app's code mode, which runs in the environment/capabilities the world exposes (also listed in its metadata).
- Expose ID's own MCP server inside the ID graph behind a flag (admin or specific user), the same way a world's MCP server can be enabled/disabled; some deployments may have no exposed MCP server except inside the iroh environment.
- Forward-looking: expose an mcpx server THROUGH ID as a world (or part of a world) — e.g. a "my laptop" world whose published functions include an MCP subset alongside other functions, so a caller can run a vector-store query on the laptop that travels MCP → mcpx → the ID server hosting the world, possibly via a relay's MCP server.

## mcpx chaining/clustering

- mcpx already has a directive to be fully self-described in its own MCP server, with access to every MCP server it can reach — confirm coverage, then add: chain/cluster connections, namespacing merged servers (five upstreams with identical command sets and random-UUID or absent names get caller-assigned namespaces: `server.a.<cmd>`, `server.b.<cmd>`, `server.c.exec(...)`), admin tools to connect/disconnect/list/inspect dynamically, and code-mode scripts that iterate and aggregate across all of them (fan out in iroh to many mcpx servers, which fan out to their local servers, reducing at each step).
- The `mcpx` namespace in our OpenCode fork's built-in tool surface: by default no direct MCP commands — just `list`, `get`, `inspect`, `exec` or similar — with admin/power-user scripts (add/remove/rename servers, aliases/namespaces, copy namespaces, per-user/global/per-session/per-execution settings changed dynamically, runtime changes written to disk persistently with backups of previous versions, shell_exec / run_exec, and shell_session — an attachable transport/socket/iroh/SSE stream that works like a shell tunnel) kept out of every agent's default view.
- Fleet's MCP variations: use the fleet tools themselves to list, extract, promote-to-root, or add servers (OpenChamber's, mcpx's, ID's) into unique namespaces as desired. Routing this through mcpx is the expected easiest path.

## Cycle safety (TODO, not V1)

Pass-through headers on chained calls, an incrementing depth count stored with the originating client, per-server max depth on received requests, basic cycle detection using initial request IDs.

## Acceptance

A design section naming: the fleet↔mcpx wiring (ports/sockets/namespace registration), the remote-graph model (aliases, promotion, depth metadata), the fan-out verb semantics (map / collect / any / first, failure handling, jq projection), ID's MCP tool surface + dynamic world attach, and the mcpx namespace/merge rules.

items.title: design(id): serverless edition storage — D1 vs Turso vs both for `id` on Cloudflare Workers

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: app/id
labels.description: Package/app: id (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/l
labels.description: Large: multi-day or open-ended; expect staged check-ins

labels.name: mode/online
labels.description: Fully doable remotely: design, config, code, cloud

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

labels.name: source/design-architect
labels.description: Filed by the repo design architect job

items.body:
## Summary

Expand #2046 (serverless edition — `id` on Cloudflare Workers) with the storage decision it left open: what is the backing store for `id` when it runs on Workers, and can the answer be more than one store?

This is a design investigation, not an implementation ticket. Its deliverable is a decision-ready comparison of **Cloudflare D1 vs Turso (libSQL) vs offering both**, a recommendation with the conditions that would flip it, and follow-on design tickets (see Decomposition sketch) detailed enough to be broken into implementation work without re-litigating the choice.

Relates to: #2046 (serverless edition on Cloudflare Workers), #806 (F12.13 journal replication — read replicas over a signed stream).

## Why this matters

The serverless edition promises `id` with no server to run. That promise lives or dies on the store underneath it:

- Every `id` invariant — identity, capability grants, journal / event history, world state — has to survive on a store whose consistency, replication, and failure model were designed for edge web apps, not necessarily for a signed, replicated journal.
- Picking the wrong store does not just cost performance; it can silently weaken the journal's guarantees (ordering, durability, replay) or lock the serverless edition into a cost / limits shape that only appears at scale.
- Conversely, supporting two stores doubles the storage-abstraction surface forever. "Both" must be justified, bounded, and priced — not adopted as an avoidance of deciding.

## Options to compare

### A. D1 only

- Native to Cloudflare: Workers binding, no extra vendor, no extra credentials for the operator.
- SQLite semantics; single-primary with read replication where available. Evaluate consistency model in detail: write consistency, read-your-writes within a session, replica lag, and what happens across regions.
- Fit for the `id` journal (#806): can the signed journal be stored, ordered, and replicated with the guarantees #806 assumes? Where does D1 replication help, and where does the signed stream have to do its own work regardless?
- Limits: database size, row / query limits, Time Travel / point-in-time recovery, backup / export story for an operator who wants to leave Cloudflare.

### B. Turso (libSQL) only

- libSQL as a SQLite fork with replication as a first-class feature (embedded replicas, primary replication). Evaluate the same consistency questions as D1, plus embedded-replica sync latency and offline behaviour.
- Fit for #806: does libSQL replication compose with — or conflict with — replication over a signed stream? Two replication systems moving the same data is a hazard to name explicitly.
- Operational shape: an external dependency and account even in the "serverless" edition; self-hosted sqld as an escape hatch; what that does to the "just deploy to Workers" story.
- Cost and limits at hobby, small-community, and large-world scales.

### C. Both — per-world or per-deployment choice

- A storage-backend abstraction with D1 and Turso as interchangeable implementations, chosen per deployment, or finer: per world.
- Price the abstraction honestly: which `id` storage operations must be in the common subset, what backend-specific features are then forbidden, how migrations between backends work (export journal → replay into the other store?), and how tests / CI cover two backends without doubling flakiness.
- Per-world choice adds a routing / metadata question: where is the "which store holds this world" fact itself stored, and what happens when a world's store is unreachable?
- State the decision rule for when "both" is worth it (e.g. operator sovereignty, an existing Turso estate, D1 limits hit in practice) vs when it is speculative generality.

## Comparison axes (required in the deliverable)

For each option, address every axis — "unknown, needs spike" is an acceptable entry, an omitted axis is not:

1. **Consistency & ordering** — write consistency, cross-region behaviour, session guarantees, ordering available to the journal.
2. **Replication / journal fit (#806)** — how store replication interacts with signed-stream replication; single-writer assumptions; conflict and fork behaviour.
3. **Cost shape** — free / entry tier, per-read / per-write / per-row pricing, storage pricing, egress; modelled at three scales (single user, small community, large public world). Include the cost of the Workers tier needed in each case.
4. **Limits & ceilings** — DB size, request / query limits, connection model from Workers, cold-start and latency profile by region.
5. **Local-dev story** — local D1 (Wrangler / Miniflare) vs local libSQL / sqld; can a developer run the full serverless edition offline? Seed / fixture / reset ergonomics; parity between local and deployed behaviour and known divergences.
6. **Durability, backup & exit** — backup, point-in-time recovery, export in an open format, migration off the platform; data-loss windows.
7. **Security & tenancy** — credentials / bindings, per-world isolation, row-level isolation assumptions, encryption-at-rest story, what a compromised Worker can reach.
8. **Operational burden** — what the operator must provision, monitor, and pay for; failure modes visible to end users.

## Non-goals

- Implementing either backend (this issue decides and decomposes; implementation is follow-on work).
- Re-designing the journal itself (#806 owns the signed-stream design); this issue only evaluates store fit against it.
- Non-serverless storage (self-hosted edition storage is out of scope except where the abstraction in option C would leak into it — flag any such leak explicitly).
- Choosing other serverless platforms (Workers is the #2046 premise).

## Acceptance criteria for the design deliverable

- [ ] A comparison document covering options A / B / C across all eight axes above, linked from this issue.
- [ ] A stated recommendation, the evidence behind it, and the conditions that would reverse it.
- [ ] An explicit statement of which journal guarantees (#806) each store preserves, weakens, or requires compensating design for.
- [ ] If "both" is recommended: the common storage contract, the choice granularity (per-deployment vs per-world), and the migration path between backends.
- [ ] Cost model at the three named scales, with assumptions listed.
- [ ] Follow-on design tickets filed from the Decomposition sketch (or the sketch revised with reasons).

## Decomposition sketch

Follow-on design tickets to be filed from this issue (indicative; revise during the work):

1. Design: storage contract for the serverless edition — the minimal `id` storage interface both backends must satisfy (journal append/read, world state, indexes).
2. Design / spike: D1 journal fit — ordering, sessions, and replication behaviour against the #806 signed-stream requirements, with a small proof of concept.
3. Design / spike: Turso / libSQL journal fit — embedded replicas and primary replication composed with #806, with a small proof of concept.
4. Design: local-dev parity for the serverless edition — Wrangler/Miniflare vs local sqld, fixtures, and the offline developer workflow.
5. Design: backend choice & migration — per-deployment vs per-world selection, where the routing fact lives, and export/replay migration between D1 and Turso.
6. Design: cost & limits guardrails — quotas, backpressure, and operator-visible warnings when a world approaches D1 / Turso ceilings.
7. Design: backup, recovery & exit for serverless storage — point-in-time recovery, open-format export, and leaving Cloudflare / Turso.

## Open questions

- Does #806's signed stream actually need store-level replication at all, or is store replication redundant (or actively harmful) once the journal replicates itself?
- Is per-world backend choice a real operator need, or is per-deployment enough? What evidence would distinguish the two?
- What is the largest world (events, state size, write rate) the serverless edition intends to support — and does either store's ceiling rule it out before cost does?
- How much D1 / Turso behaviour can only be learned from a running spike vs vendor documentation, and which claims in the comparison are documentation-only?
- If both are supported, who owns keeping the second backend honest — CI matrix, contract tests, or manual verification per release?
- Does Turso's self-hosted sqld option blur the line between the serverless and self-hosted editions in a useful way, or create a third, accidental edition?

items.title: impl(id): keyless-custody login — OIDC account-pointer binding and OPAQUE password login over a client-held ID key

items.body:
## Summary

Implement the keyless-custody login chosen by the #5885 feasibility record and assigned to parent #5684 to file: **OIDC (Google) as an account-pointer binding and OPAQUE (RFC 9807) for username/password, both over one random, client-generated, client-held ID signing key.** The authorizer never possesses or can use the user's ID signing key.

Design of record:
- Parent synthesis: `doc/2026-11-23T20-55-00Z_design_id5684_identity_login_synthesis/` (#5684), especially §4 (signed-hash construction), §5 (feasibility matrix), §11.
- Feasibility + invariants: #5885 decision record (2026-11-08).
- Genesis artefact it builds on: #5884 `SetupStatement` (`doc/2026-11-08T23-17-06Z_design_id_setup_ceremony/`).
- Custody variants it serves: #5887 (b, user-held blob), #5889 (d, pseudo-login grants).

## Scope

1. **Login binding enrolment:** client signs the `"id/login-binding/v1"` binding statement (ID public key, auth issuer + subject hash or OPAQUE account identifier, custody profile, recovery commitment hash); authorizer verifies and stores the public key, statement, and signature. Binding updates require a signature from the existing ID key or the #5888 recovery threshold — an authenticated OIDC session or a password reset is never sufficient.
2. **OIDC flow:** authorization-code flow with PKCE; ID Token validated (issuer, audience, signature, expiry, nonce); `(iss, sub)` used as the account pointer only. Login success fetches ciphertext artefacts; it never by itself authorises an ID operation.
3. **OPAQUE flow:** an audited OPAQUE implementation for username/password; the random ID key is wrapped client-side under a key derived from the RFC 9807 `export_key`; the server stores the OPAQUE registration record and ciphertext only. The server OPRF seed is handled as high-entropy secret material (name only; never in code, logs, or this repo's artefacts).
4. **Challenge verification:** for ID-authorised operations (login acceptance where the ID key is required, new-device enrolment), the authorizer issues a fresh nonce/audience/expiry-bound challenge; the client-held ID key signs; the authorizer verifies against the bound public key. New-device enrolment additionally names the requested pseudo-login scope in the signed challenge (composition with #5887 §4.3 and #5889).
5. **Composition with existing code:** `pkgs/id/src/key_envelope.rs` already provides the local Argon2id/XChaCha20-Poly1305 passphrase envelope; reuse it for the wrapped-key storage rather than introducing a parallel envelope. Current `AccountSignedUp`'s bearer-secret key reconstruction is explicitly **not** a precedent for this work (#5885).

## Invariants (test oracles — from #5885)

1. The authorizer never receives the unwrapped ID private key.
2. Auth success alone never registers/replaces an ID key or expands delegation.
3. Every key-binding/recovery mutation is signed by the current key or an explicit recovery threshold.
4. Server-stored backup is ciphertext, and its offline-guessing assumptions are disclosed in user-facing copy.
5. Password reset and OIDC-account recovery are never represented as identity recovery.
6. Delegation stays least-privilege, expiring, revocable, with pseudo-login provenance preserved in raw records (full delegation implementation is the separate #5889 slice; this issue must not mint standing delegations outside it).

## Non-goals

- The custody-variant implementations themselves (setup ceremony #5884 §13, variant (a) signing service, variant (b) blob UX, recovery codes #5888, grants #5889, management UX #5890) — named as the parent synthesis §11 programme; this issue is the login layer they compose with.
- Acting as an OIDC *provider* (that is #13658's workstream, a different direction).

## Filing note (queue coverage)

Filed by lane felix from the #5684 parent synthesis (queue task 21487), per the tracked next action in #5885's decision record. Enqueued to the code pilot queue in the same pass by the filing lane.

# Provider self-renewal audit — 2026-11-09

Drew's rule (2026-11-09 20:42 CST): **all the providers renew themselves.** Every OAuth/token credential must refresh itself automatically; a provider dying on an expired token because renewal was missing, mis-targeted, or unprovisioned is a defect. Tonight produced three instances of that defect class — openai.main (sync wrote to the wrong door; fixed, fork PR #2237), _claude (credential blanked Nov 7; restored by hand), _antigravity (client secret never provisioned; fixed, PRs #8098/#8099). This audit checks **every** door against the rule so the class is closed, not just tonight's three instances.

Method (all reads 2026-11-10 ~02:45–03:00Z, laptop, generation 551, fork build ff9858a = deployed HEAD): live config pair `opencode.jsonc` (17 providers), credential store (24 rows, metadata only — no values read), deployed source (`packages/core/src/credential/codex-sync.ts`, `packages/core/src/integration.ts` resolve path, `packages/ai/src/providers/*-auth.ts`, `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/{openai,opencode}.ts`), CLI credential files (timestamps/lengths only), route_attempt serving evidence (last 24h), quota gatherer records.

## How renewal works in this fork (the two paths)

- **In-provider refresh:** `Integration.connection.resolve` refreshes any stored OAuth credential within 5 min of expiry, when its method implements `refresh` — **unless** the credential is stamped `externalRefresh`, in which case an external owner is the sole refresher (by design, to avoid rotating a shared refresh-token lineage twice).
- **External-owner sync:** CodexSync runs every 1 min, copies `~/.codex/auth.json` into the stored credential **whose account ID matches the file's account** (selectTarget), and stamps it `externalRefresh`. One account's tokens are never written into another account's credential.

## Per-provider table

| openai.alternate | OAuth (ChatGPT, Student) | credential row `cred_17514e9…` | In-provider refresh at resolve (openai plugin implements refresh for both methods). Deliberately NOT CodexSync's target — different account than the CLI file | **SELF-RENEWS (proven)** | Row refresh-write 2026-11-04T22:05:48Z (expiry +10d exactly) during continuous service; 2,175 successful attempts in the last 24h on that lineage; no externalRefresh stamp | 2026-11-14T22:05:48Z (auto-refreshes at resolve) |
| opencode-go.popesdrew | OAuth (Console) | credential row `cred_1a1bd3e0…` (base `opencode` row is the same lineage, same expiry) | In-provider refresh at resolve (opencode plugin implements refresh, writes back the rotated pair) | **SELF-RENEWS-UNPROVEN** | Mechanism in deployed source; row untouched since creation 2026-11-04 — no refresh event has occurred yet. Acceptance check: row `time_updated` advances on first resolve at/after ~2026-12-03T17:37Z with no human step | 2026-12-03T17:42:29Z |
| opencode-go.drewrypope | API key | credential row | — | **NO-RENEWAL-NEEDED** | 3,296 successes / 24h | — |

Acceptance check: file mtime/expiresAt advance past the access expiry with no human or CLI step. | google (OAuth row `cred_12e4e76…`) | OAuth | credential row | Door disabled in config; access token expired 2026-10-12, refresh token still held | **DORMANT** — not serving; no live defect. If the door is ever re-enabled, first resolve must be watched: the row has been expired for a month | Row untouched since 2026-10-12 | access expired 2026-10-12T05:10:53Z |
| github-copilot | OAuth | credential row + auth.json | Door disabled in config | **DORMANT** — not serving | Last success 2026-10-24 (legacy id) | none recorded |
| opencode (base row) | OAuth | credential row | Disabled integration; same token lineage and expiry as opencode-go.popesdrew | **DORMANT duplicate** of the popesdrew door row | Identical expiry to the second (2026-12-03T17:42:29Z) | 2026-12-03T17:42:29Z |

## Findings

1. **Zero CANNOT-RENEW defects among live doors.** After tonight's three fixes, every serving door either self-renews, holds a static key, or has a configured renewal that has not yet had its first natural test.
2. **Three SELF-RENEWS-UNPROVEN doors, each with a dated acceptance check:** opencode-go.popesdrew (first refresh due at the 2026-12-03 expiry approach), _claude (first rotation due at the 2026-11-10T10:28:53Z access expiry — today), _muse (re-mint unobserved; account-token expiry uninstrumented, watched by the meta-renewal validator). If any acceptance check fails, it becomes a CANNOT-RENEW defect on sight.
3. **Hygiene observations (not renewal defects):** (a) the legacy `claude-code` credential row holds stub-length tokens from 2026-10-05 and the legacy provider id drew 9 auth-failing attempts in 24h (last 2026-11-10T00:14Z, pre-restore) — the live _claude door never reads this row; recommend deleting the stub row and retiring the legacy id. (b) The dormant `google` OAuth row (above). (c) The base `opencode` row duplicates the popesdrew lineage.
4. **Quota-side browser sessions are a separate surface**, already owned by #6120 (OpenDesign keeper landed; Meta portal re-capture requirement sits on #6079; ClinePass dashboard adapter dormant by design). This audit covers serving credentials; #6120 covers the monitoring reads. Cross-linked, not duplicated.

## Acceptance for closing this audit

- [ ] _claude: file rotation observed past 2026-11-10T10:28:53Z with no human/CLI step (or a defect filed the same day).
- [ ] opencode-go.popesdrew: row refresh observed at the 2026-12-03 expiry approach (or a defect filed the same day).
- [ ] _muse: a re-mint/exchange event observed in serving, or the account credential gains an expiry record a watcher can alert on.

items.body:
# Hosted worlds & always-on hosting — Phase 14 core topic (research + design)

Filed from the next-horizons discussion #1240, decided by Drew on 2026-11-05: **all themes are planned**. This issue is the core topic for **Hosted worlds & always-on hosting**. Its job is research and design — broaden the idea beyond what is already understood, set up multiple next steps, and produce implementation plans. No implementation starts here; the output is design documents and implementation issues.

## Drew's principles for everything in Phase 14 (from #1240, 2026-11-05)
- Local-first is always the goal, AND a hosted version is intended: central coordination supporting a large graph of broadly accessible objects.
- Anything built must be completely usable by others hosting a small or large server themselves. P2P-hosted worlds and data behave the same as a large hosted public server; differences live in backend scale elements and access controls.
- Users connect to each other and transfer/interact directly wherever possible, so hosted resources are an offloadable backstop, not a requirement. The app must not technically need us to function. Collaborative / shared / federated / local-first / p2p.
- Our hosted instance is essentially public; other operators open theirs only as much as they want. Publishing paths: share to a big server, publish on pkarr, or self-host. All comms through iroh on the backend; first-class clients.

## The idea, broadened
A world today lives while a host process runs. Hosting asks: what is a world when nobody is connected? Broaden beyond 'run the same binary on a VPS': world persistence semantics, who may wake/pause a world, journal custody and backup, operator trust, and how a hosted world stays the *same object* as the local one (same journal, same programs, same ceilings) so moving a world between a laptop, a home server and a public host is a transfer, not a port. Include the split Drew named: a totally public main endpoint, with deeper backend pieces as separate iroh/id servers behind private tunnels with limited trusted access.

## Research questions (first pass)
- World lifecycle states (live, asleep, archived) and who can transition them under the role model (Phase 10 roles, F12.3 authority frames)
- Journal custody: encryption at rest, snapshot/export formats, restore drills — what 'backup' means for a journaled world
- Basement cluster as the first hosting target: capacity, power/egress limits, what breaks first
- Hosted vs local parity checklist: which behaviors must be identical, which are legitimately backend-only (quotas, abuse controls, storage tiers)

## Dependencies and existing pieces
Builds on F12.11 multi-node worlds (#805), F12.13 journal replication (#806), F12.10 quotas (#1067), #227 journal rollback compatibility (done). First Phase 14 implementation theme (with discovery).

## Next steps — the version ladder
- **v1 — first-iteration design** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v2 — outline: custody & lifecycle** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v3 — outline: many nodes** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below
- **v4 — outline: public-server operation** — its own issue, filed in the same pass and linked in the first comment below

Plus a standing rule for this topic: anything the research surfaces that doesn't fit v1–v4 gets its own issue (Drew's rule: every feature, concept, or idea gets an issue), and future investigations are listed as comments here rather than lost.

## Sequencing
Design queue order: F12.4 provider registry (#1061) and F12.10 scheduling/quotas (#1067) designs land first; Phase 14 v1 designs then run hosted worlds → discovery → agents spike → the rest. Implementation follows Phase 13. The drop rule applies throughout: anything that proves blocked, wrong, or superseded gets parked or closed with a note — never a silent stall.

items.title: feat(fleet): registry transport offers + github-backup deploy tests skip without node
items.body:
Before: the #2179 machine registry had no way to say which transports a host serves or which agents may use them. Separately, the github-backup deploy tests crashed with a Python traceback on any machine without `node`, and three placement tests on main still assumed the old 15-minute watchdog cadence, so they failed.

After: each host record can carry `transports` (offers with kind, endpoint data and credentials by name only) and `enrollment` (which agent classes may use which offers). amd-6 now lists its four current legs. The deploy tests print a clear SKIP line when `node` is missing, and CI sets `GITHUB_BACKUP_REQUIRE_NODE=1` so a missing node there still fails. The placement tests derive staleness from the watchdog's own `STALE_AFTER_SECONDS`.

**#14714 (transport pooling design §1.2, work item 1a)**
- `scripts/validate-fleet-machine-registry.py` accepts the optional `transports` and `enrollment` fields and rejects:
  - an unknown transport kind;
  - a credential value in place of a name (long digit-bearing tokens, `_`, `:`, `/`, `=`, capitals, or mappings);
  - extra secret-looking keys beside an offer or in its endpoint;
  - URLs carrying userinfo or a query string;
  - enrollment entries that name offers the record does not have.
- `doc/fleet-machine-registry.yaml`: amd-6 gets four offers (commander door, laptop-agent via Cloudflare, the daemon over the tailnet, real SSH) and enrollment for opencode lanes, Muse seats and external MCP clients.
- 14 new tests, including YAML round trips of a fixture and of the shipped registry.
- No consumer changes. The watchdog rewrites only the health block, and placement reads only capabilities, capacity and health.

**#14267**
- The three `infra/github-backup/tests/test_deploy_*.py` files check for `node` before they run.
- The workflow's regression step sets `GITHUB_BACKUP_REQUIRE_NODE=1`.

**Placement tests (main was red)**
- The watchdog cadence moved to 30 minutes, so staleness is now 60 minutes. `test_stale_health_reads_as_left`, `test_tier_1_before_tier_2_then_ineligible` and `test_committed_registry_view_matches_its_cache` still used 30, and failed on main. They now read the window from `watchdog.STALE_AFTER_SECONDS`.

Fixes #14714
Fixes #14267

items.title: cold-store-reaper v3: backup retention (prune-backups), get-backup, backup-d1, nightly + drill scripts
items.body: Extends pkgs/cold-store-reaper (v1 #923, v2 #929, sync fix #933) with the DESIGN §5/§8 operator layer: **Commands** - `prune-backups [--db ] [--apply]` — retention **30 daily / 12 weekly / 12 monthly** per db-backups/ folder, computed as a pure function of the listing (filename timestamps, newest-first; no wall clock). Keep set = union of newest-per-day (30 distinct days) + newest-per-ISO-week (12) + newest-per-month (12). Unparseable names are never pruned (reported skipped). Dry-run by default; `--apply` trashes via files.update {trashed: true} — never a permanent delete — and writes one transfer_ledger row per file (direction `trash`, kind `backup-prune`). - `get-backup ` — exact-name lookup, full download, prints size + sha256. - `backup-d1` — deterministic SQL export of the D1 cold-store-manifest database via the REST query API (shared `_d1_endpoint`/`_d1_select` helpers refactored out of sync-manifest), filed through put-backup. **Schema note**: the `trash` ledger direction extends the transfer_ledger CHECK (schema.sql, marked v1.1). Existing local manifests are migrated in place on first open (table rebuild preserving rows, covered by a test). The D1 copy of the schema needs the same one-line change before prune rows can sync — until then sync-manifest surfaces D1's own error text. README documents this. **Scripts** (bash, shellcheck-clean, chmod +x, secrets via env only) - `scripts/nightly-backup.sh` — backup-d1 → prune-backups --apply → sync-manifest → status; fails loudly. - `scripts/restore-drill.sh` — §8 quarterly drill: 3 pseudo-random cold objects fetched through the production rehydrator Worker with sha256 verification; newest d1 backup loaded into in-memory SQLite, per-table row counts compared against live D1 (local manifest fallback). Per-item DRILL PASS/FAIL + verdict, non-zero exit on failure. Failure paths smoke-tested locally. **Tests**: 26 passing (17 prior + 9 new), 1 skip (node worker-decoder, node_modules unavailable in sandbox — same as v2). Fake Drive gains PATCH/trash + trashed-aware listings + full-media downloads; Fake D1 can answer SELECTs from a backing sqlite DB. Highlights: hand-computed 37-file retention scenario with exact keep/prune sets and reasons; --apply trash calls + ledger rows; 400-day history bounds; backup-d1 export loads back byte-identical (quote escaping, NULLs); pre-v3 manifest migration. --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added commands to export D1 databases to Drive backups and download individual backups. * Added backup pruning with a default preview mode. Applying pruning moves older backups to Drive trash while retaining recent backups across daily, weekly, and monthly periods. * Added scripts for nightly backups and restore checks, including verification of stored objects and database backup contents. * **Documentation** * Added usage examples and guidance for backup, pruning, and restore workflows.
