Survey taken 2026-10-30 on the laptop (`amd`), ordered by Drew alongside the muse-proxy direct-mode NixOS pass. Cross-refs: #2753 (direct mode), #2104 (proxy-supervisor retirement / per-proxy HM units), #1752 (PM hand-unit gaps — see status note below), #883 (stale-tree ExecStart trap).

## Phase A result (today's stack)

The muse-proxy / muse-direct stack was already declarative — no functional change was needed:

- `systemd.user.services.muse-proxy` in `home/common/default.nix` (#2104) generates exactly the live unit: evaluating this flake at origin/main yields ExecStart `/nix/store/7bxcdg21iqjmiinxh0bl92kyjwrbmkdn-muse-proxy-start-unit`, byte-identical to the running unit, and `nixosConfigurations.amd` evaluates clean end to end.
- The unit runs `bin/muse-proxy-start.sh` from the live checkout (egress unpinned, `META_API_KEY` unset by the script); direct mode reads `~/.config/muse/auth.json` at runtime — the credential is never in the config. The `muse-direct` provider lives in `.opencode/opencode.jsonc` with `baseURL http://127.0.0.1:{env:MUSE_PROXY_PORT:-18747}/v1`, the port defined once as `museProxyPort` in `home/common/default.nix`.
- PR #2774 (merged, `4189b191`) only extended the unit comment so the NixOS source of truth records direct mode; re-evaluation after the edit produces the identical ExecStart, so nothing is superseded at activation and no restart is implied. There is no remaining activation step for this stack beyond the next ordinary rebuild.

## Headline finding: the retired fleet-proxy-supervisor's units are still alive

#2104 retired the supervisor and made the per-proxy Home Manager units the sole owners of the canonical ports. In reality, seven `fps-*` transient units (started via `systemd-run`, no supervisor process exists) are still running, and four of them hold canonical ports, so their declarative replacements crash-loop:

| Port | Listener today | Declarative unit state |
|---|---|---|
| 18742 clef | `fps-clef-proxy-18742` (since 2026-10-28 20:57) | `clef-proxy` auto-restart, 1,170 restarts, exit 1 |
| 18743 agy | `fps-agy-proxy-18743` (since 2026-10-28 13:02) | `agy-proxy` auto-restart, 1,168 restarts, exit 1 |
| 18745 antigravity-ls | `fps-antigravity-ls-proxy-18745` (since 2026-10-28 20:57) | `antigravity-ls-proxy` auto-restart, 1,169 restarts, exit 1 |
| 18749 claude-code | `fps-claude-code-proxy-18749` (since 2026-10-28 13:05) | `claude-code-proxy` auto-restart, 1,169 restarts, exit 1 |
| 19744 / 19746 / 19748 | `fps-codex-proxy-19744`, `fps-design-code-proxy-19746`, `fps-commandcode-proxy-19748` (all since 2026-10-29 23:08) squat the +1000 alternates | canonical ports correctly held by the declarative units |

The proxies themselves also still write `~/.local/state/<proxy>/endpoint.json` (fresh timestamps, incl. muse-proxy at its 09:30 restart today) — the files are live state written by the proxy processes, not just stale supervisor records as the #2104 comment assumes.

## Services & proxies inventory

### Fleet proxies (all user units; code in `bin/`, run from the live checkout)

| Service | Port | Managed today | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| muse-proxy | 18747 | HM unit, `home/common/default.nix`; running, direct mode live | Already declarative — done (#2774) |
| codex-proxy | 18744 | HM unit + **hand drop-in** `codex-proxy.service.d/warm-override.conf` overriding ExecStart to the checkout | Remove the drop-in: post-#2104 the unit already runs the checkout, so the #480-era override is redundant |
| design-code-proxy | 18746 | HM unit, running (fps twin on 19746) | Already declarative; kill the fps twin |
| commandcode-proxy | 18748 | HM unit + **hand drop-in** `commandcode-proxy.service.d/fix-execstart.conf` pointing ExecStart at `~/git/code/bin/...` — the *other* checkout | Remove the drop-in: it is the #883 stale-tree trap in live form; the HM unit already runs `~/code/bin/commandcode-proxy-start.sh` |
| opencode-route-proxy | 18750 | HM unit, running | Already declarative |
| clef-proxy | 18742 | HM unit declared, crash-looping behind fps transient | Stop the fps unit at a natural break; unit then owns the port |
| agy-proxy | 18743 | same | same |
| antigravity-ls-proxy | 18745 | same | same |
| claude-code-proxy | 18749 | same | same |
| proxy-supervise.mjs (fps) | — | Retired in flake (#2104); 7 transient units still running; config fossils in `~/.config/proxy-supervisor/*.bak/.unmanaged-20261026`; `bin/proxy-supervise.mjs.new` tracked leftover | Retire fully: stop transients, delete fossils after |

### Core AI services

| Service | Port | Managed today | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| openchamber | 3000 (tailnet) | HM unit, `home/common/default.nix` + **hand drop-in** `openchamber.service.d/external-opencode.conf` (attaches to the external OpenCode server; sets `OPENCODE_HOST`/`OPENCODE_SKIP_START` and a password env var) | Convert the drop-in into the flake (or fold into the unit) so the external-opencode arrangement survives a config regeneration |
| opencode serve (standing server) | 13420 | **Bare process** (session scope, PPID 1, started 2026-10-30 09:18 from a shell) | Leave alone operationally (session-bearing); backlog: give it a declarative unit at a natural break — it is the process OpenChamber and the fleet's sessions depend on |
| mcpx | 34543 | HM unit, `home/common/default.nix` (+ `mcpx-reload` path unit) | Already declarative |
| t3code | 3773 | HM unit, `home/common/default.nix` | Already declarative |
| openclaw-gateway | 18789 | HM unit, `home/openclaw/default.nix` | Already declarative |
| desktop-commander-remote | — | HM unit, `home/common/default.nix` | Already declarative |
| sync-models | timer | HM unit + timer, `home/common/default.nix` | Already declarative |

### PM stack & apps

| Service | Port | Managed today | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| pm-projector | — | User unit declared via `nixos/services/pm-stack/default.nix` | Already declarative |
| pm-aggregator | 4870 (tailnet) | same | Already declarative |
| pm-dispatch | 4879 (tailnet) | same | Already declarative |
| pm-tunnel (cloudflared) | 20241 metrics | same — this is the machine's running cloudflared; `nixos/services/cloudflared/` only documents manual tunnel setup | Already declarative; tidy the cloudflared module comment to point at pm-tunnel |
| pm-git-sync, pm-dashboard-backup, pm-projector-reconcile, quota-gatherer | timers | Declared via pm-stack / laptop-backups modules | Already declarative |
| docker-pm-grist / docker-pm-kaneo / docker-pm-pad / docker-pm-postgres | 3000 / 7777 / 8484 area (tailnet; owning pids not visible without sudo) | System units, NixOS-generated from `nixos/services/pm-apps/default.nix` (oci-containers) | Already declarative — **#1752 looks substantially landed**; verify and close or re-scope it |
| ready-for-agent | 6056 (0.0.0.0) | User unit declared via `nixos/services/pm-apps/default.nix`, binary from the pm-stack deployment dir | Already declarative (see #1752 note above) |
| pm-kaneo (user unit) | — | Declared (pm-apps/pm-stack), timer-driven companion to the docker app | Already declarative |

### Automation, backups, quota exporters (user timers/services)

| Item | Managed today | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| laptop-autocommit-{hatch,hatch-personal,openclaw}, laptop-repo-keeper, laptop-untracked-review | HM via `nixos/home/laptop-autocommit.nix` / `laptop-repo-keeper.nix` | Already declarative |
| atlas-backup, openclaw-backup, supabase-backup, repo-archive-backup, cold-store-{nightly,drill}, agent-backup | HM via `nixos/home/laptop-backups.nix` / `home/common/default.nix` | Already declarative |
| meta-quota-export (svc+timer) | **Hand-made files** in `~/.config/systemd/user/` | Convert to HM (same pattern as sync-models) |
| cloudflare-quota-export (svc+timer) | **Hand-made files** | Convert to HM |
| dashboard-backup (svc+timer) | **Hand-made files** | Convert to HM (alongside pm-dashboard-backup) |
| oc-password-sync (svc+path) | **Hand-made files** | Convert to HM, or fold into the openchamber declaration |
| git-maintenance@ (svc+3 timers) | Hand-placed copies of git's upstream template | Leave alone (upstream template) or declare via HM for completeness |
| rustdesk (user svc) | **Hand-made file** (ExecStart from `/etc/profiles/per-user/...`) | Convert to HM or leave; low value either way |

### System services (NixOS)

sshd, tailscaled, docker, dnsmasq, `id-primary` (`nixos/services/id-mail`), `power-guard` (`nixos/services/power-guard`), display-manager/desktop stack — all NixOS-generated from this flake. Already declarative; no action.

### Bare processes (no unit)

| Process | Port | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|
| `python3 -m http.server 8899` | 8899 on 0.0.0.0 | Identify owner; retire (world-bindable directory server) |
| `python3 /tmp/mock.py` | 18777 | Retire (test mock) |
| `pkgs/id` debug build demo (`~/git/code/pkgs/id/target/debug/id --data-dir ~/id-demo-data`) | 3210 | Retire or replace with the packaged build; demo data dir |
| node `~/git/fleet/2900-394-proxy-c…` | 36539 | Identify; retire or promote to a declared proxy |
| `/tmp/mcpxdbg/mcpx daemon --detached` | 38481 | Retire (debug instance; the real mcpx is a unit) |
| opencode serve | 13420 | See Core AI services — leave alone, backlog a unit |

### Fossils & leftovers (inert, delete after the fps stop)

- `~/.config/systemd/user/proxy-supervisor.{service,timer}.unmanaged-20261026`, `~/.config/proxy-supervisor/config.json.unmanaged-20261026` + two `config.json.bak-*`
- `*.backup` / `*.bak-*` unit files next to pm-aggregator, pm-git-sync, pm-projector, quota-gatherer, repo-archive-backup, ready-for-agent units (inert, but they confuse every future survey)
- Tracked in git under `bin/`: `codex-proxy.mjs.pre-warm-20261024`, `codex-proxy.mjs.resume-build.bak`, `commandcode-proxy-start.sh.bak-20261025003957-netfix`, `muse-proxy.mjs.bak-20261024-flag-tolerance`, `muse-proxy.mjs.bak-20261024121323-laptop-deploy`, `proxy-supervise.mjs.new`
- Hand drop-in `app-com.mitchellh.ghostty.service.d/overrides.conf` (desktop app; noted for completeness)

## Conversion checklist

- [ ] Stop the 7 `fps-*` transient units at a natural break so the 4 crash-looping declarative proxy units take their canonical ports; confirm `systemctl --user` shows exactly one owner per proxy port afterwards
- [ ] Remove `codex-proxy.service.d/warm-override.conf` (redundant post-#2104)
- [ ] Remove `commandcode-proxy.service.d/fix-execstart.conf` (#883 trap; points at the wrong checkout)
- [ ] Fold `openchamber.service.d/external-opencode.conf` into the flake declaration
- [ ] Declare meta-quota-export, cloudflare-quota-export, dashboard-backup, oc-password-sync in Home Manager
- [ ] Verify #1752 against pm-apps (docker-pm-* + ready-for-agent are declared and running) and close or re-scope it
- [ ] Retire the stray bare processes (http.server 8899, /tmp/mock.py, mcpxdbg, id demo, fleet proxy experiment)
- [ ] Backlog: a declarative unit for the standing `opencode serve` (:13420), landed only at a natural break
- [ ] Delete the fossil unit/config files and the tracked `bin/*.bak` leftovers
- [ ] Fix the #2104 comment in `home/common/default.nix`: endpoint.json files are still written by the proxy processes themselves

## Sandbox (out of scope for conversion)

The sandbox VM is not NixOS-managed: its services are `~/tools/init.sh` `run_step`s (mcpx-service, opencode-service, muse-proxy-service, agy/commandcode/claude-code proxy services, proxy-supervisor-service, …), several deliberately disabled or stubbed by Drew's 2026-10-25 pass. Listed only so this survey is complete; no conversion is proposed.

---

*Method: `systemctl --user`/system unit + timer listings, `ss -tlnp` port→pid→cgroup mapping, unit FragmentPath/file-type checks, and flake-source grep on the laptop, 2026-10-30. Nothing was stopped, restarted, or reconfigured during the survey.*

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each `fps-*` transient unit squatting a canonical port (18742, 18743, 18745, 18749) is stopped and its declarative Home Manager replacement is running and stable (no crash-loop) on that port, or the item is split into per-proxy follow-up issues naming the blocker.
- [ ] The +1000 alternate-port squatters (19744, 19746, 19748) are cleared or explicitly documented as intentional.
- [ ] Hand drop-ins and hand-managed units in the inventory (e.g. codex-proxy warm-override) are either converted to declarative config or recorded as deliberate exceptions with a reason.
- [ ] The endpoint.json state files are documented as live proxy-written state (the #2104 assumption that they are stale supervisor records is corrected wherever it appears).
- [ ] A post-change survey re-run shows no `fps-*` transient proxy units remain, and the result is posted on this issue.

items.title: github-backup(worker): /queue/ack body is shape-trusted — null/non-JSON/string-ids crash the handler, a top-level array fakes acked:0, non-string ids delete wrong keys; and one corrupt KV value crashes every GET /queue

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

items.body:
## Problem

The github-backup queue Worker's two authenticated drainer endpoints parse JSON with no shape guard, so a malformed request or a single corrupt queue entry crashes the handler (an unhandled throw in a Worker = a bare 500) or, worse, reports a successful ack that deleted nothing / the wrong keys.

File: `infra/github-backup/worker/src/index.js` (verified on main `8a5cd8ea75`)

### 1. `POST /queue/ack` — the request body is shape-trusted (:87-88)

```js
const { ids } = await req.json();
const keys = (ids || []).map((id) => "ev:" + id);
```

Verified with the real file verbatim (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-ghb-worker-ack`, node v24, stubbed KV; control `{ids:["a","b"]}` → 200 `{acked:2}`, deletes `ev:a`,`ev:b`):

| Body | Result today |
|---|---|
| `null` | **throws** `TypeError: Cannot destructure property 'ids' ... as it is null` |
| non-JSON (`not json`) / empty body | **throws** `SyntaxError` from `req.json()` |
| `{"ids":"abc"}` / `{"ids":123}` | **throws** `TypeError: (ids \|\| []).map is not a function` |
| top-level array `["a","b"]` | 200 `{"acked":0}` — a **fake success**: the caller's ids are silently dropped, nothing is deleted |
| `{"ids":[123,null]}` | 200 `{"acked":2}` — deletes the wrong keys `ev:123` / `ev:null` and reports success for ids that never existed |
| `{}` (missing `ids`) | 200 `{"acked":0}` — indistinguishable from a legitimate empty ack |

The ack is the drainer's delete path (`infra/github-backup/bin/drain_queue.py` `ack_events`, :86-97): events are acked only once the mirror reflects them (#3219 discipline), so an ack response that lies about what it deleted undermines the one signal the drainer has that the queue actually shrank.

### 2. `GET /queue` — one corrupt KV value crashes every poll (:76)

```js
if (v) events.push(JSON.parse(v));
```

Verified: with one stored value `not-json{`, `GET /queue` throws `SyntaxError` and returns nothing — every event on the page is lost to the drainer, and because listing is what feeds the ack path, the corrupt entry can never be acked away through the API. The values are normally written by this Worker's own webhook handler (:46-52, whose `JSON.parse` **is** guarded — the in-file twin), but KV is shared, mutable state: a manual edit, a future writer, or a partial write leaves a permanent poison pill in the queue. This is the Worker-side mirror of the drainer-side poison pill in #6575.

The existing test suite (`infra/github-backup/worker/test/index.test.mjs`) covers only well-shaped ack bodies (`{ids:["a","b","c"]}`) and well-formed KV values — none of the cases above.

## Why it matters

- A malformed ack (a buggy/manual caller, a truncated request) produces an opaque 500 instead of a 400 the caller can act on.
- The top-level-array and non-string-id cases are worse than a crash: they return 200 with a count that does not describe what was deleted, so a drain can believe events were retired when they were not (or that foreign keys were).
- One corrupt KV entry wedges the whole queue for the drainer: no listing, no acking, no self-healing path through the API.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `POST /queue/ack` with a non-JSON, empty, JSON-`null`, or non-object body returns a 4xx with a clear error message; no exception escapes the handler and no KV delete is attempted.
- [ ] `POST /queue/ack` with `ids` missing, not an array, or containing a non-string/empty entry returns a 4xx naming the `ids` field; a well-formed `{ids:[...]}` behaves exactly as today (bulk-chunked deletes, `{acked: n}`).
- [ ] An ack response's `acked` count always equals the number of keys actually deleted.
- [ ] `GET /queue` with one corrupt (non-JSON) KV value does not lose the whole page: either the well-formed events are returned with the corrupt key named/signalled in the response, or the endpoint fails with an error naming the corrupt key — never a bare `SyntaxError` 500. (Either disposition is acceptable; silently dropping the entry without any signal is not.)
- [ ] New cases in `infra/github-backup/worker/test/index.test.mjs` cover: null body, non-JSON body, string `ids`, top-level array body, non-string id entries, and a corrupt KV value on `GET /queue`; the existing 5 tests still pass.

items.title: fleet-paperwork: two GitHub page loops have no page bound (#6622 contract rule 2)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

items.body:
## Gap found by the #6623 closing pagination inventory (Phase 4 of #6622)

The pagination contract (#6622, rule 2) requires every page loop to carry a page-count or accumulated-result bound whose breach is an error naming the listing. Two GitHub page loops in `infra/fleet-paperwork/fleet_paperwork.py` follow pages with `while True` and no page bound:

- `AppClient.installations()` (fleet_paperwork.py:262-283): pages `/app/installations?per_page=100&page=N`, stopping only at a short/empty page.
- `AppClient.assert_repo_in_scope()` (fleet_paperwork.py:312-339): pages `/installation/repositories?per_page=100&page=N`, stopping when the accumulated count reaches the response's `total_count` or a page is empty.

Both terminate against GitHub's real API (finite listings; a page past the end is empty/short, and the second is also bounded by the server's own `total_count`), so this is a contract-conformance gap, not a live hang: a fresh-full-page stream (buggy or hostile endpoint, or a proxy fault) loops unbounded, accumulating results, instead of ending in a diagnosable error naming the listing — the exact shape #6602/#6572 bounded in cold-store-reaper and github-backup.

The third page loop in the same file, the issue-search scan (fleet_paperwork.py:403), is already capped (`for page in range(1, 11)`, the Search API's 1000-result ceiling) and conforms.

## Fix shape

Add a generous named page bound to both loops (sized off the legitimate maximum: installations and per-installation repositories for the orgs the App serves), whose breach dies with an error naming the listing — mirroring `MAX_QUEUE_PAGES` in github-backup's drain_queue.py and `MAX_PAGES` in fleet-dispatch-test's `fetch_all_pages`. Add a test with a fake transport that always returns full pages, asserting the bound fires (the probe matrix on #6622 includes the fresh-token stream past the bound).

Filed by the #6623 closing inventory per its acceptance rule: a gap is filed as its own issue, never fixed silently inside the inventory.

items.title: Atlas repo docs and design archive disagreements: README index, who serves, CI triggers, census freshness, endpoint table (book survey, #13251)
items.body:
Found by the Atlas book survey (#13251, survey D). Disagreements in the repo's own Atlas documentation and design archive. The book (pkgs/atlas-search/book/) now carries the reconciled account; these are the stale sources.

1. **doc/README.md indexes 6 Atlas records; doc/ contains 38 Atlas entries.** Most of the design archive — including the design of record, scaler revision, staging gate, classification, metadata, D1-cache and embedded-replica records — has no README entry, while one README entry (the lawyer packet) has no "atlas" in its directory name. A reader navigating by the README misses ~85% of the archive. (The book's roadmap chapter now maps all 38.)
2. **Design-of-record layout vs the package as built.** Design §4 proposes pkgs/atlas-search/ with a package-local doc/ and exactly four crates + fixtures/. The built package has docs/ (plural, three files), no package-local doc/, and substantial extra top-level surface the design tree does not show (atlas_search.py, worker/, eval/, schema/, tools/, tests/, test-vectors/, onnxruntime/).
3. **atlas_search.py points at a README that was not there; Python line count drift.** The Python header says "(see README.md in this directory)" — pkgs/atlas-search/ had no README.md (the book PR adds one, so the pointer now resolves). The design of record describes the Python as 1,177 lines (true of the hatch-personal copy); the in-repo copy is 1,629 lines. The two copies are not the same file version; "the Python reference" needs a which-copy qualifier.
4. **Who serves: design + unit name say atlas-search serve; the live ExecStart is fleet serve search** (#5604, atlasSearchServeViaFleet = true). The Worker README's deploy note ("a binary refresh of the laptop's atlas-search.service") is unit-accurate but binary-silent on this point.
5. **CI headers/names vs CI triggers (three workflows).** atlas-search-pr.yml is named for PRs but triggers on nightly schedule + dispatch only (deliberate policy; the name is the stale part). atlas-search-worker-tests.yml's header says it runs "on pushes to main that touch pkgs/atlas-search/worker/ and on dispatch"; its on: block is dispatch + nightly only. fleet-search-parity-guard.yml presents as a drift guard for a byte-parity contract but triggers on workflow_dispatch only — nothing runs it automatically, and the two server.rs copies already differ in size (151,924 vs 151,913 bytes), so "verbatim copy" in fleet-search/src/lib.rs reads as a maintained copy under parity discipline, not byte-identity.
6. **Program record names a package that does not exist.** The program investigation record describes "`pkgs/atlas-search/`, `pkgs/atlas-core` surfaces" — there is no pkgs/atlas-core; atlas-core is a crate inside pkgs/atlas-search/crates/.
7. **Two caches, opposite TTL stories, both called "the Atlas cache".** The service temp store: in-memory, 10-minute TTL / 60-minute hard cap, nothing survives restart by requirement (a security property). The Worker cache (#6805): Durable-Object-persisted, indefinite, no TTL/eviction in v1 (a cost property). Documents that do not name which store a TTL claim belongs to mislead; the book names them separately throughout.
8. **Embedding endpoint 18791 (memory design) vs in-process ONNX (everything else).** The memory-integration design routes ingestion embeddings through "the openclaw-embedding service, fixed loopback port 18791" or atlas-embed. No code, nix, or other doc in the Atlas estate references 18791; the built embedding is in-process ONNX resident in the serve process, and the service's outward embedding surface is POST /v1/embed on :18760 (#6788). The memory design's slice 2 does not describe the pipeline the service runs.
9. **Ingest: two generations described as current in different homes.** The turso-atlas README presents the collect→normalize→index→publish→access atlas-ingest.py pipeline as THE pipeline, present tense. The in-repo machinery describes per-unit staging DBs, a registry, classification-at-staging, an M6-gated promote and a five-stage batch gate; the scaler design's migration table says the aggregator path replaces direct-to-core ingest. The 2026-11-23 program record sides with the README on current practice (manual/script-driven; #5670 migration open) and with the in-repo design on target shape. The book states the generation labels once, early.
10. **Census freshness: the headline numbers are a 2026-10-31 snapshot repeated as present tense.** 18,325 / 122,124 / 107,639 appears in the design of record (2026-11-04) as current shape and is still the ground-truth line in the 2026-11-23 program record — which itself flags the store has grown (~7.3 GB monolith) without a verified recount. The design of record's "107,639 chunks in a Turso database" (monolith framing) and the program record's "monolith plus 29 topic shards" describe the same census at different physical-layout generations. The book dates the census 2026-10-31 everywhere.
11. **Design endpoint table vs the implemented route table.** Design §2's table has seven rows; the implemented server.rs dispatch adds POST /v1/embed, POST/GET /v1/feedback (+ unversioned aliases) and GET /v1/search/jobs. None contradicts the design, but an API chapter built from the design table alone would omit three live surfaces — including the one the Worker depends on.

Book chapters: pkgs/atlas-search/book/design/roadmap-and-issue-map.md (archive map), reference/service-api.md, concepts/ingest.md, operations/backup-and-census.md.

items.body:
## What this is

Drew, 2026-10-29: find where OpenClaw's own scheduled tasks can replace Muse tasks, with management and monitoring of those tasks and outcomes. Study + live smoke test: ~/workspace/research_notes/openclaw-scheduled-tasks-20261029/findings.md. Companion to #2171 (setup + job passing + the OpenCode comparison review).

## Verdict: the scheduler is fleet-grade and idle

- Gateway live and healthy (user service since 2026-10-28 20:43 CDT, HTTP 200, OpenClaw 2026.10.7).
- `openclaw automations` (alias `cron`) is a full scheduler: cron/every/at/on-exit/stream schedules; agentTurn / command / script payloads; isolated or bound sessions; per-job model, fallbacks, thinking level; announce/webhook/no-deliver delivery; failure alerts after 2 consecutive failures; backoff, catch-up runs, restart reconciliation.
- Ledgers live in ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite (cron_jobs, cron_run_receipts, task_runs) — status, duration, error, summary. **No token columns**: token review must join each run's session transcript/agentMeta, and OpenClaw usage never enters the runtime DB — migrated jobs leave the Supabase export's attribution unless the ledgers get bridged (that bridge is #2072 work).
- Today exactly two managed jobs exist (hourly heartbeat-main; Memory Dreaming Promotion). No fleet work has ever been scheduled through it. The heartbeat currently SKIPS hourly (`heartbeat skipped: no-route` — no channel binding for main) and inbound webhooks are disabled (POST /hooks/agent → 404).

## Smoke test (2026-10-29, first job ever passed — review row #1)

- Route: `openclaw agent --agent main --session-key smoke-20261029 --json`. One real blocker found and cleared: a bare SSH shell cannot resolve the gateway token SecretRef; the documented fix is exporting OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN from ~/.secrets/openclaw/gateway-token (value through process env only).
- Result packet: outcome ok (runId a323dfd6…), **13,746 input / 237 output tokens, $0 recorded, 11.8s gateway time** (74s wall including CLI startup at laptop load ~20). Answer quality good with one honest gap (described fleet peers from workspace docs instead of enumerating the actual second gateway agent, `opencode`).
- **KEY CATCH: the agent's configured primary — commandcode/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash — failed 401** (the still-pending Command Code sign-in) and the run succeeded only by falling back to design-code/deepseek-v4.1-flash. Gate: fix the Command Code sign-in or repoint the primary before relying on OpenClaw runs.
- Cost shape for the review: a watchdog-class periodic digest costs ~376K Claude input tokens per run on Muse; an equivalent OpenClaw isolated run costs ~14K pool tokens and **zero** Muse subscription tokens (different budget, not free — pool quota).

## Migration candidates

1. **Watchdog-class periodic digests** (read-only synthesis over local state) — the cost shape above.
2. **Laptop-local read-only monitors** — quota/pool reads, backup verification: the data is already on the laptop; a Muse cron pays subscription tokens to go read it remotely.
3. **Deterministic script checks as command payloads** with webhook delivery — no model tokens at all unless a check trips and escalates to an agentTurn.
4. **OpenClaw housekeeping** — already native; extend rather than rebuild.

Poor candidates: queue worker shifts and anything whose product is a GitHub write under Muse's review loop (see #2174 for the OpenCode side).

## Gates before scheduling fleet work here

1. Command Code 401 resolved or the agent primary repointed (config change rides the NixOS switch path).
2. Channel bindings or --no-deliver/webhook delivery chosen per job (heartbeat no-route skip is the symptom).
3. Token bridge: cron_run_receipts/task_runs joined to session usage and exported into Supabase, so the #2171 review (outcome/tokens/time vs OpenCode) covers scheduled runs too.
4. Inbound webhooks enabled if event-triggered OpenClaw jobs are wanted (ties to the repository_dispatch bridge in #2176).

## What #1728 + the switch do and do not do

Config today: ACP enabled with exactly one allowedAgent and one acpx agent (opencode). The merge + switch expands allowedAgents to [opencode, claude, codex, agy] with per-agent command overrides in both the embedded acpx config and ~/.acpx/config.json — that turns OpenClaw into a dispatcher that can hand coding work to ACP harnesses (and later the muse harness, #2012) instead of only running its own native turns. It does NOT fix the gateway-token env, hooks, channel bindings, or the Command Code 401.

## Acceptance

- Gates 1–3 closed; first two candidate classes running as OpenClaw scheduled jobs for a week, each run reviewed (outcome/tokens/time) against its Muse-cron baseline on #2171's comparison.

items.body:
Split from #2381 (encrypted identity backup) as the design-first half. The local envelope half is #2279; the seed-phrase half stays on #2381.

## Problem
#2381 proposes a passphrase-wrapped identity backup stored server-side, with a memory-hard KDF and a rate-limited *blinded* unwrap (OPRF-style) so the server can throttle guessing without learning the passphrase or the key. Nothing of that exists at main `048da81f1`:

- No backup blob format anywhere in `pkgs/id/src` (`grep -rln "backup"` hits only `world_doctor.rs`, `repl/input.rs`, `currency_poc/tests.rs`, `web/routes.rs`, `cli.rs`).
- No OPRF or blinded-unwrap primitive anywhere in `pkgs/id/` or `doc/` (`grep -rli "oprf\|blinded"` → no matches).
- The identity key is still the raw file `KEY_FILE = ".iroh-key"` (`pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:314`).

Implementing this without a recorded decision would invent a wire format, a server-side key-custody posture and an unwrap-throttling protocol in one PR.

## What this design must settle
1. **Blob format** — AEAD + KDF versioned envelope (reuse #2279's header shape rather than defining a second one), keyed by identity-public-key hash; server stores ciphertext bytes only.
2. **Server-side custody posture** — restate that the server never holds plaintext or passphrases, and what it does hold (ciphertext, size, access timestamps). #2060's trust constraint still forbids custodial keys.
3. **Unwrap throttling** — whether an OPRF-style blinded unwrap is adopted, which curve/construction, and how throttle state is keyed so it reveals nothing. If OPRF is rejected, record the cheaper alternative (e.g. per-identity attempt budget over the existing fixed-window limiter shape from #2333) with its guessing-cost analysis.
4. **Storage surface** — which hosted storage the blob lives in, retention, and deletion on key revocation.
5. **Restore-forces-rotation** — the flag's representation, which is #2380's keyset substrate.

## Acceptance
- [ ] A decision is recorded on this issue for items 1–5, or each is explicitly deferred with rationale.
- [ ] The server-never-sees-plaintext claim has a concrete protocol sketch (who computes what) that a reviewer can falsify.
- [ ] Follow-up implementation issues are filed from the decision, or the decision is to decline the server-side backup entirely.

## Out of scope
- Local envelope export/import (#2279), seed-phrase export/restore (#2381), guardian/social recovery (#2382), issuer key rotation (#2804).

## Sources
`doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted/` §4, §7, §11 slice 2; #2060 (closed); #2279; #2380; `pkgs/id/src/lib.rs:314`.


## Acceptance criteria

- A design is recorded settling: the backup blob format (AEAD + KDF versioned envelope, reusing #2279's header shape), the blinded-unwrap (OPRF-style) protocol, server-side rate limiting / throttling, and the server key-custody posture.
- The design names what the server learns and cannot learn (passphrase, key, blob contents) for each protocol step.
- An implementation issue is filed and linked as a native relation in the same pass the design lands (protocol §11 — a design with no implementation link is not finished work).

items.title: github-backup(deploy): advertise the configured version as the rollback target (#3475)
items.body:
Fixes #3475. Queue task 5425 (lane C); sibling task 5424 / PR #3480 (#3474, same file) already merged — this builds on that deploy.mjs state, no competing PR.

## Problem
- Normal flow: deploy uploaded version → `setWorkerSecrets()` → advertise `version.id`. But `wrangler secret put` creates and deploys a **new** version carrying the bindings, so the advertised version was the pre-secrets upload — rolling back to it restores a Worker without `DRAIN_BEARER` / `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`.
- `--deploy-version <id>` deployed the version and exited without ever provisioning/verifying runtime configuration.

## Change (`infra/github-backup/worker/deploy.mjs`)
- Normal flow: after provisioning, re-read the live deployment (`liveVersionIds()`) and advertise the **final configured version** as live / rollback target, with a note line when it supersedes the upload.
- `--deploy-version`: **verify before deploying** (revised in the Codex round — see the reply on the P1 thread). A historical version's configuration cannot be added after the fact: ordinary `secret put` hard-errors with `VERSION_NOT_DEPLOYED` when the latest version isn't deployed (the rollback state by definition), and `versions secret put` patches the *latest* version, not the selected one (both verified against the pinned Wrangler 4.147.0 source). So the path reads the target's bindings via `wrangler versions view --json` and refuses, *before* any traffic switch, a target missing the required secret bindings — naming the roll-forward remedy. Configured targets (including every version the fixed normal flow advertises) deploy as-is.
- No credential values in arguments, logs, or artifacts (secrets pass via wrangler stdin only, as before). No live deployment was run.

## Tests (laptop, stubbed executables — no network, mock values only)
- New `infra/github-backup/tests/test_deploy_rollback_version.py` — **16/16**: stateful wrangler stub modelling secret-put creating a new live version; normal flow advertises `configured-final` (not the upload) on the `live:` line; rollback of a configured target verifies bindings before deploying and needs no secret put; rollback of an unconfigured target is refused (non-zero, missing bindings named, no deploy attempted); mock secret values never appear in stdout/stderr.
- Existing suite: `test_deploy_dry_run.py` 11/11 (stub now answers `versions view` with a configured version), `test_drain_queue.py` 54/54, `test_inventory_owner.py` 18/18, `test_reconcile_retention.py` 9/9. `node --check` clean.

items.title: feat(aggregator): archive audit events before retention pruning + backup/restore evidence (#3322)
items.body: Implements the remaining issue #3322 audit-history scope (task 13199, lane code-x): the retention/archive/backup-restore remainder after PR #5137 (audit v2) and PR #5141 (ingestion). ## What lands - **Archive-before-prune retention contract** (`pm-stack/aggregator/src/events.ts`): both retention bounds (30 days / 5000 records) now flow through one gate, `partitionRetention`. Records leaving the hot stream are first appended — deduplicated by stable id, in stored-chain order, with their original hashes — to monthly partitions under `events.json.archive/` (`events-archive-YYYY-MM.json`). If an archive write fails, pruning is deferred and `health()` reports it; a record is never dropped unarchived. A chain that fails verification is never laundered into the archive, and never-chained records drop only with a loud log. - **Archive integrity + visible gap**: `verifyArchivedRecords` recomputes every archived record's hash; partitions are re-verified before every merge-write. `health()` gains `archivedRecords`, an `archive` verdict, and `historyGap` — when the hot chain's retention anchor names a pruned predecessor no partition holds (pre-contract pruning, a lost partition), the gap is a named field, not a silent hole. - **Backup set** (`nixos/home/pm-dashboard-backup.sh`): every generation now stages and manifest-records `aggregator/events.json.outbox.jsonl` (when present), the `aggregator/events.json.archive/` tree, and `aggregator/activity-ingestion.json`, alongside the already-required `events.json`. No #1514 database-backup duplication. - **Docs**: `pm-stack/aggregator/docs/audit-event-retention.md` — limits, integrity rules, backup set, and the restore procedure. ## Restore evidence (new tests, `test/events-archive-3322.test.ts`) - Load-path pruning archives records byte-identical to what was stored; the archive verifies after a restart, with contiguous links from genesis. - Append past the bound is archived, not dropped; count and time bounds both split through `partitionRetention` with pruned = oldest, in stored order. - A tampered archive partition fails the archive health verdict; a pre-contract anchored chain reports `historyGap.present`. - Full round trip: a fixture state (hot events + archived history + a pending retry in the outbox + ingestion checkpoints/seen IDs) is copied into a manifest-verified generation (sha256 + size per file, all four audit members present), restored into an isolated dir, and shown to recover — outbox flushed with no duplicates, retained chain verifies, archived history intact and not duplicated into the hot stream, and replaying the same activity deliveries yields `ingested: 0, duplicates: 2` with the stream unchanged. Issue #3322 stays open per its own instruction ("do not claim the overall #3322 issue complete until the audit-specific backup/restore evidence exists") — this PR supplies that evidence for review; the queue task completes as pr_opened with the evidence attached. Refs #3322 --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.

items.title: laptop-autocommit-openclaw death spiral: 131MB live sqlite tracked in git, push can never succeed, ~10 cores burned every minute

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: status/parked
labels.description: Deliberately paused with a recorded resume condition

labels.name: queue/parked
labels.description: Queue task is parked (waiting on CI, time, or an event)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

items.body:
## Symptom

The laptop (16 cores) sits at sustained load ~25–28. `laptop-autocommit-openclaw.service` fires every minute and each run consumes 8–13 CPU-minutes in ~62 s of wall clock with a 9–17 GB memory peak, then fails: `autocommit: PUSH FAILED in /home/user/.openclaw (N commit(s) unpushed)` — N grows by one every minute (2205 at 12:55 CST → 2406 at 16:23 CST on 2026-11-15). The `.git/objects/pack/` dir is littered with `tmp_pack_*` garbage from killed pack runs (151 garbage files, 556 MB).

This permanent load is the amplifier behind the PM aggregator page flaps tracked in #9850: with the box saturated, aggregator assemblies starve. It contributed to the 2026-11-14 attention.json flaps and to the post-#10466-deploy /board 503 on 2026-11-15 16:16 CST (cold caches after the 16:12 switch restart + a /board assembly that blew the 10 s deadline under load ~26, with no last-good cache to serve stale from).

## Evidence (2026-11-15, laptop, live reads)

- `journalctl --user -u laptop-autocommit-openclaw`: every minute `Consumed 8min–13min CPU time over ~1min wall, 9.5–16.9G memory peak`, followed by `PUSH FAILED ... unpushed` with the count incrementing by 1 per run.
- Repo state: `git count-objects -vH` → 8603 loose objects, **6.19 GiB loose**; `@{u}..HEAD` = **2406 commits ahead**, never draining.
- Largest tracked file: `agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite` = **137,469,952 bytes (131 MiB)** — a live SQLite DB rewritten continuously, re-hashed and re-stored as a fresh loose blob by `git add -u` every minute. Second: `state/openclaw.sqlite` 8.2 MB, same churn pattern.
- The push can never succeed: the 131 MiB blob exceeds GitHub's 100 MB per-file hard limit, and the script's `timeout 60 git push` kills pack-objects mid-compression every run — pack threads on all 16 cores for 60 s, every minute, forever. A death spiral: each failed run adds one more commit and one more ~131 MB blob to the next attempt.
- The other three autocommit units are healthy (hatch-personal: 1.4–3.6 s CPU/run) — this is specific to the `.openclaw` repo contents, not the script's other deployments.

## Scope

- `~/.openclaw` checkout of dezren39/openclaw-personal on the laptop, and `laptop-autocommit-openclaw.{service,timer}`.
- NOT in scope: the aggregator/projector code (#9850 / PR #10466 covers that side; its reconcile + attention fixes verified live 2026-11-15 16:15 CST — a full pass now takes ~16 s / 58 rows vs 22–35 min / ~11.5k rows before).

## Fix applied (ops, this pass)

1. Stopped `laptop-autocommit-openclaw.timer` to stop the bleed.
2. Backup coverage check: the daily `openclaw-backup` job already archives all of `~/.openclaw` (sqlite DBs snapshotted transaction-consistently) to local + R2 + Drive with 30-day retention — untracking the live DBs from git loses no backup coverage; they never reached GitHub anyway.
3. Preserved the local tip under `refs/backup/pre-squash-2026-11-15`, untracked both live sqlite DBs (`git rm --cached`) + added them to `.gitignore`, squashed the 2406 unpushed autocommits into a single commit on top of `@{u}` (tree = current tracked state minus the DBs; no blob >100 MB), pushed, restarted the timer.

## Acceptance

- `laptop-autocommit-openclaw` runs complete in seconds, push succeeds, `@{u}..HEAD` returns to 0 after each cycle.
- Laptop load average returns to normal (well under core count) with the timer running.
- Aggregator probes (/board, /api/attention.json, /api/quota.json) sustain 200s with no timeout/503 over a 15-minute window under the restored timer.

## Follow-ups worth considering

- A guard in `pkgs/laptop-autocommit`: refuse (loudly, once) to commit a tracked file over ~95 MB instead of spiralling — defense in depth for every autocommit deployment.
- `git gc` on the `.openclaw` repo to reclaim the ~6.2 GB of unreachable loose objects once the fix verifies.

Refs: #9850 (aggregator stalls — this was a contributing load source), #1723 (autocommit program, closed).

items.body:
Relocated from dezren39/nix#504 on 2026-10-28 - it was filed in the wrong repo; developing-today/code is its home. Original content follows, verbatim.

---

## Problem

Design and validate the cluster's storage before the hardware is committed. Drew's sketch (from the register — to be validated, not assumed): three tiers across 3 hosts, replicated with DRBD + LINSTOR so that **data loss needs the same failure on 2 machines at once**.

Source: [idea register 2026-10-20](https://github.com/dezren39/hatch-personal/blob/main/workspace/goals/stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs/files/idea-register-2026-10-20.md) (goal `stand-up-lab-cluster-talm-talos-cozystack-postgres-rustfs`).

## Drew's sketch

- **HDD tier (cold-ish RustFS buckets):** 3 hosts × 4 × 16 TB helium WD drives in **RAID 10**. (15–16 drives exist in total.)
- **Fast NVMe tier:** all Samsung 990 Pro.
- **Mid NVMe tier:** 980s, smaller 990s, good consumer SSDs — stripe 3 (≈ 990-class aggregate performance) × mirror 2 = **6 drives ("RAID 100": 3 stripes, 2 mirrors)**, so two drives must die to take down a machine.
- Two named pools from earlier work: (1) 4 drives RAID 10; (2) 6 drives RAID 100 (3 stripes × 2 mirrors).
- Goal: 3–5 devices with near parity in disk size and capability.
- Consumers: RustFS (S3) on the HDD tier; Postgres (CloudNativePG) and general volumes on NVMe tiers; LINSTOR/DRBD for cross-machine block replication.

## Acceptance / first steps

- [ ] Map the validated hardware inventory (see inventory issue) onto the three tiers: exact drive counts per host, usable capacities per pool.
- [ ] Decide the layering: md RAID vs LINSTOR/DRBD-native striping/mirroring vs ZFS — and where each pool's redundancy actually lives (in-host vs cross-host), checking the "2 machines must fail" claim against the design.
- [ ] Benchmark the mid tier's 3-stripe claim against a single 990 Pro (does striping 980-class drives actually reach parity?).
- [ ] Define failure drills: pull a drive, pull a host; measure rebuild time/impact on 16 TB members.
- [ ] Emit the result as declarative per-node storage config feeding the TALM bootstrap issue.

## Open questions

- NIC throughput between core hosts (pending inventory) — caps DRBD replication and rebuild speeds.
- RustFS erasure coding across hosts vs RAID 10 under it: one redundancy layer or two?

## Acceptance criteria

- A storage design is recorded on this issue (or a linked design doc/PR) validating or revising the three-tier sketch (RAID10 HDD / fast NVMe / mid NVMe with DRBD + LINSTOR).
- The design states the replication/failure model: which single-machine failures are survived with no data loss.
- Drive counts are reconciled against the actual inventory (see #1810) before any purchase/commitment.
- Follow-up implementation issues are filed and linked for any build work.

items.body:
Drew's directive, 2026-11-04: documentation and designs that are **not strictly about the sandbox environment** move their canonical home from dezren39/hatch-personal + dezren39/hatch into this repo; darwin-nix keeps only flake documentation. items.title: kaneo unreachable: aggregator sign-in fails with 500 (pre-existing)
items.body:
## Observed

The PM board reports, verbatim:

    kaneo unreachable: kaneo sign-in failed (500)

## Where it surfaces

- Thrown by the aggregator live Kaneo source:  —  when the Kaneo sign-in request returns a non-OK status (observed: 500) or no session cookie.
- Surfaced to the board as the  source error, so the Kaneo lane of the board shows no live data while this persists.

## Timeline

Pre-existing: observed on the board before 2026-11-04 and unrelated to the 2026-11-03/04 decommission and quota-board work. No existing open issue covers the sign-in 500 (searched 2026-11-04: 26 open issues mention kaneo — backups, SSO design, host migration — none track the sign-in failure).

## First investigation steps

1. Check the Kaneo service itself (container/host health) — is the 500 from Kaneo or from a proxy in front of it?
2. Check whether the aggregator sign-in credentials/endpoint drifted (Kaneo upgrade, auth change) vs. Kaneo being down.
3. Decide whether the board should degrade more quietly while a source is unreachable, separately from fixing the sign-in.

items.title: docs(id): Turso/libSQL journal fit decision record (#5865)
items.body: ## Summary Decision record for #5865: how Turso/libSQL replication composes with the #806 signed journal, under the #5681 direction landed today (BOTH with roles — Turso preferred, embedded replicas on endpoints; the signed journal is the system of record, every store a materialisation). ## The decision - The signed stream is the only journal replication. libSQL replication (embedded replicas, primary replication) is a materialisation accelerator inside one deployment/trust domain and confers no journal authority. - An embedded replica is a cache with a freshness bound: its content is presentable as world state only up to a verified (ordinal, digest) cursor. - Writes go to the primary only, from the single journal writer; replica write-forwarding is never used for journal appends; a replica is never promoted to writer (failover is a journal-layer chain-base decision). - Journal-to-libSQL mapping: `journal_entry` (exact entry bytes, `(world_id, ordinal)` PK) + `journal_head`, batch append and snapshot/reset as single transactions; access over the HTTP pipeline (house precedent: `foreign_libsql.rs`), keeping the native dependency guard intact. ## Spike Executed (§6.1 of the record): the table mapping against the SQLite engine libSQL forks — ordinal-ordered storage, byte-exact `entry_bytes` round-trip, duplicate-ordinal refusal by the PK, single-query head-consistency check. Owed (§6.2): embedded-replica frame-sync behaviour (latency, offline reads, backwards-head convergence). Not executable on the fleet laptop today — no `sqld` installed (`turso dev` refuses to start), and the `turso` shell is a CGO-disabled stub. Filed as follow-on spike #8346 with the record's acceptance verbatim. ## Invariants & conflicts Seven implementation invariants (§5), including fork refusal when the primary's head digest diverges from the verified chain. Parent-conflict check (§8): none — #5681, #5869, and #806 decisions are consumed unchanged. Closes #5865 --- Open in [code]smith · Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **Documentation** * Added an architecture decision record describing how signed journals and libSQL replication fit into the system, including write, verification, reset, and export requirements. * Documented SQLite-core findings and noted that embedded-replica sync behavior remains to be validated. * Added the decision record to the architecture index.

items.title: story: our own OIDC/SAML/SSO identity provider
items.body:
## User story

As the operator of our own services, I want one self-hosted identity provider issuing OIDC + SAML SSO for our own services — pm-stack, the mcpx and Desktop Commander doors ([#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404)), OpenChamber, fleet surfaces — so that sign-in across our estate runs on our own identity instead of a patchwork of third-party IdPs and per-service arrangements.

Motivation:

- One identity: the same person, service, and policy across every service, instead of a separate account story per service.
- Our own trust anchor: signing keys and certificates issued from our own PKI, under our own control, instead of trusting a vendor's keys for our own estate.
- No per-service vendor dependency: adding a service means registering a relying party with our provider, not adopting another third-party IdP or inventing a one-off sign-in scheme.

Done at the story level looks like: our provider is the sign-in path for at least one service of each class in the acceptance criteria below, its signing keys come from our PKI and can be rotated without breaking sign-in, and a new service can be onboarded by configuration against our provider rather than by choosing a new identity vendor.

This story does not start from a blank page. It is the story-level frame over the SSO program that already exists — parent issue [#9077 — parent SSO program issue itself](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9077) and its children — plus the PKI foundation and the SAML scope, which the existing program does not cover. The "Prior work and references" section below is the map; the slice plan builds on those pieces rather than re-specifying them.

## Scope + acceptance criteria

- [ ] PKI foundation exists: root CA, an issuing intermediate, and cert-generation tooling (Slice 1).
- [ ] OIDC discovery + JWKS signing works: the provider publishes its discovery document and a JWKS signed from PKI-issued keys.
- [ ] SAML IdP metadata + signing works: the provider publishes signed SAML IdP metadata and signs SAML responses.
- [ ] At least one relying party from each class signs in end-to-end: a web app, and a CLI/API surface.
- [ ] Signing-key rotation is demonstrated: a new signing key is published and trusted, and the old key is retired, without breaking sign-in.
- [ ] Operators can issue and revoke service certificates from the PKI.
- [ ] Provider accounts bind to pkgs/id accounts via the binding ceremony in [#2852 — hosted provisioning SSO ID binding](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2852) (recorded as acceptance debt in the provider child issue, not an afterthought).

## Prior work and references

Search record (2026-11-23, GitHub issue search over developing-today/code, counts confirmed from the search API): `oidc` 222 hits, `saml` 4, `sso` 71, `"identity provider"` 73, `idp` 20, `oauth` 170, `login` 301, `auth` 1185. The `login`/`auth` counts are broad and noisy; the relevant hits are below.

**Plain findings first:**

- **SAML is new ground.** All 4 `saml` hits are the github-backup estate mirror and GitHub-org SAML access — no prior SAML IdP design, issue, or design record found. The SAML scope in this story is genuinely new work, not a re-specification.
- **Number corrections to the original brief for this story:** the Google federated-login issue is [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412), a child of #9077. [#12412 — console gate whole public hostname](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/12412) is a closed PR (the pm-stack console as the gate for the whole public hostname), related to the Access wiring but not itself a Google-login issue. And [#8299 — id roles capability ceiling config](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8299) is pkgs/id role configuration (capability ceilings, delegation bounds), not mcpx work — the mcpx ceiling/session line is [#1902 — mcpx daemon ceiling caller lowers](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1902), [#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950), and the mcpx book's identity chapter (below).

### The existing SSO program — #9077 and its children

- [#9077 — parent SSO program issue itself](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9077) — SSO for fleet services: GitHub/Google/Microsoft login gated to Drew + a devtoday OIDC provider with roles + account linking. This story's OIDC half is that program, framed at story level and extended with PKI + SAML.
- [#13409 — minimal devtoday OIDC provider standup](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13409) — standard OIDC issuer (code + PKCE), JWKS + key rotation, Drew-only allowlist enforced in the provider, #1253 role claims, no id keypair custody in the login path.
- [#13411 — GitHub federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13411)
- [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412)
- [#13414 — Microsoft federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13414)
- [#13415 — account linking flow with history](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13415) — one account, every door, with retained identity history.
- [#13416 — first consumer proving full loop](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13416) — first consumer integration (PM stack) proving the full loop.
- [#13417 — fleet SSO provider decision note](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13417) — the decision note PR for #9077; it settles the pkgs/id question (see the design questions below). Open at filing time; its design record is `doc/2026-11-23_design_fleet_sso_9077.md` on its branch until merged.
- [#9086 — hosted editions consume SSO design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9086) — hosted editions are relying parties consuming #9077; tenancy accounts aligned with #1253 roles.
- [#1253 — one identity across the stack](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1253) — SSO propagation from the public entry into every layer; the four-role model (owner / orchestrator / agent / read-only) is the consumer-side contract the provider's claims must carry.
- [#1182 — dashboard behind Cloudflare Access design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1182) — the settled Access model for the pm-stack entry; the existing door this provider eventually stands behind.
- [#9605 — stack token minting exchange work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9605) — stack-token minting + agent token-exchange under #1253; how an entry session becomes per-layer tokens.

### pkgs/id — the existing identity system

- [#2056 — ID platform expansion epic home](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2056) — the ID program epic; pkgs/id is Drew's identity system (Iroh-key identity, id-caps capabilities, directory, groups).
- [#2852 — hosted provisioning SSO ID binding](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2852) — external SSO identities bound to pkgs/id accounts (spec source #2258); slices 1–2 landed, 3–4 open at last record in #9077.
- [#5684 — identity login delegation design work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5684) — identity, login & delegation: key custody, security-code recovery, pseudo-login identities. Its custody questions are unresolved, which is part of why the provider does not start inside id.
- [#2060 — key recovery versus SSO loss](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2060) — the standing rule from the key-recovery investigation: SSO authenticates a person to an account record; it never rebinds an identity key.
- [#2380 — keyset authorization log identity substrate](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2380) — device keys, revocation, and bindings as signed records; the revocation/rotation substrate Slice 5 builds on.
- [#8299 — id roles capability ceiling config](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/8299) — roles as first-class world config: capability ceiling, delegation-lifetime bounds, grant/revoke as audited events. The id-side role/ceiling model the provider's roles must not silently diverge from.

### Doors, mcpx, and fleet token auth — worked examples and neighbours

- [#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404) — Worker front door, Access gate, laptop bridge.
- [#13488 — OAuth front door shipped implementation](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13488) — merged PR: OAuth 2.1 front door for hosted MCP clients (`pkgs/desktop-commander/worker/src/oauth.ts`). The in-house worked example of the OAuth pattern.
- [#12417 — Google OAuth client creation task](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/12417) — the Google OAuth client for pm.security.cab; the concrete Google-side wiring the Access door runs on today (closed).
- [#12412 — console gate whole public hostname](https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/12412) — closed PR: the pm-stack console is the gate for the whole public hostname.
- [#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950) — mcpx as OAuth client / resource server. Per `doc/fleet/mcpx-oauth-authorization-server.md` (decision 2026-10-28), mcpx does **not** embed an authorization server — it points at external ones. This provider is the external server it points at.
- [#13657 — mcpx public endpoint front door](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13657) — mcpx public endpoint with an OAuth/Google-SSO front door and machine bearer; a first-class relying party candidate for this provider.
- [#1902 — mcpx daemon ceiling caller lowers](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1902) — the capability-ceiling mechanism (daemon sets, caller may lower, never raise) that provider-issued policy/session claims must respect.
- [#5343 — laptop agent resident execution design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5343) and [#5362 — queue secrets brokers laptop design](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/5362) — the fleet/laptop-agent token-auth line: brokered, token-gated laptop services reached only through the session proxy. The machine-to-machine auth pattern the provider's CLI/API relying parties should align with, not replace casually.
- [#9158 — fleet CA canonical secrets model](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9158) — fleet-ca canonical secrets model, provider adapters & custody policy; adjacent to Slice 1's PKI — the CA program links #9077 and does not absorb it (per its design record below), and this story returns the favour.

### Design records (repo `doc/`)

- `doc/2026-11-23_design_fleet_sso_9077.md` — the #9077 decision note (via PR #13417, on branch until merged): settles separate-minimal-provider-first, with an explicit fold path into pkgs/id.
- `doc/2026-10-30T22-45-00Z_design_hosted_provisioning_sso_binding.md` — hosted provisioning + SSO→ID binding spec (#2258 line): Google SSO authenticates the account; the Iroh root key is the identity.
- `doc/2026-10-28T23-34-14Z_investigation_cloudflare_workers_fit/` — §4: Google SSO on Workers and binding a Google identity to an ID identity; "SSO is the door; the ID key remains the identity"; custodial keys rejected.
- `doc/2026-10-29T11-28-18Z_investigation_key_recovery_hosted/` — key recovery for hosted users; verified at the time that pkgs/id contained no Google/OIDC/OAuth/WebAuthn code — all SSO content was specification.
- `doc/2026-11-10T23-58-00Z_design_pm_stack_identity/` — the #1253 design record: Access JWT at the entry, short-lived stack tokens per layer, roles in the aggregator registry, "the central OIDC provider (#9077)".
- `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2046.md` + `doc/2026-11-01_design_id2283.md` — hosted-edition identity designs; they record an unresolved conflict with the Oct 30 SSO spec (`binding_id` vs `sub` as the store key) that the design pass must reconcile, not rediscover.
- `doc/fleet/mcpx-oauth-authorization-server.md` — mcpx embed-vs-point-at decision: hybrid, point-at-first; mcpx never issues tokens, it validates other issuers' tokens via JWKS.
- `doc/2026-11-13T01-34-11Z_design_fleet_ca_credentials_secrets/` — the fleet CA / credentials / secrets program: its note links #9077 as an adjacent relying-party/identity program it does not absorb; its spec (§27) already compares Keycloak / Authentik / Kanidm / Zitadel for a standalone SSO platform — the build-vs-adopt design pass starts from that comparison, not from zero.
- `doc/2026-11-12T19-10-07Z_design_keyset_authorization_log/` — the #2380 keyset/authorization-log design.
- `pm-stack/console/README.md` — records today's wiring plainly: `google.access-sso` OAuth client secrets, the Access sign-in method, and "the central OIDC provider (#9077)" as the intended provider.

### The four books

- **id book** (`pkgs/id/book/`): `concepts/identity-directory.md` (Identity, the directory and groups), `concepts/capabilities.md` (Capabilities, ceilings and providers), `design/identity-directory-groups.md` (identity, directory, groups and delegation), `design/hosted-editions.md` (hosted and serverless editions), `design/capabilities-providers.md`. This is where id's identity model is written down as a book, and the fold-path design must be written against it.
- **mcpx book** (`pkgs/mcpx/docs/`): `spec/identity.md` ("Who an MCP request is from"), `compare/register/auth.md` (the authorization register: OIDC discovery, PKCE, issuer checks), `decisions/0007-elicitation-identity.md` (elicitation binds no user identity), and the auth rows of `spec/conformance-matrix.md`.
- **fleet book** (`pkgs/fleet/book/`): `concepts/proxy.md` (Proxy, sessions and recovery) and `reference/queue-dispatch.md` are the closest chapters — the fleet book covers sessions and tokens as transport, and **no dedicated SSO/identity chapter was found in the fleet book**.
- **atlas book** (`pkgs/atlas-search/book/`): `design/fleet-and-id-integration.md` and `design/access-evolution.md` touch ID integration and access evolution; **no prior dedicated identity, federation, or sign-in design was found in the atlas book**.

### Sandbox-side notes

- `~/memory/topics/id-program-2026-10-28.md` — Drew's ID program directive: the Workers edition signs in via Google SSO, Google `sub` is the SSO key, custodial keys rejected.
- Standing operator practice (memory, 2026-10-24): SSO-first sign-ins for Drew's own service accounts — operator practice, not IdP design, listed here so the two are not conflated.
- No SAML material was found in the sandbox notes either — consistent with the GitHub search: SAML is new ground on every front searched.

## Open design questions — options and chosen defaults

Chosen defaults below are recorded under Drew's decision posture: prefer options, "both" where both can coexist, and the more capable option over the most locked-down or most basic. Where a prior decision already exists, it is recorded as the chosen default rather than re-decided.

### 0. Relationship to pkgs/id — the central question

pkgs/id **is** an identity system (Iroh-key identity, capabilities, directory, groups; epic #2056). Any new provider has to state its relationship to it:

- **Option A — Same system:** pkgs/id itself becomes the OIDC/SAML provider.
- **Option B — A layer over it:** a thin OIDC/SAML protocol layer whose accounts and keys are id accounts and id keys throughout.
- **Option C — Deliberately separate first, with a fold path:** a separate minimal provider now; provider accounts later bind to id accounts via the #2852 ceremony, with an explicit path for the provider to fold into id.
- **CHOSEN: Option C — separate minimal provider first, explicit fold path into pkgs/id.** This is the decision already recorded in the #9077 decision note (PR #13417; Drew may override per §5 of that note). Reasoning, from #9077's own evidence: no OIDC surface exists in pkgs/id, #5684's key-custody model is unresolved and more exotic than a conventional issuer, #2852's binding slices 3–4 are open — while fleet services need boring, standard OIDC first. Two standing constraints bind whichever option the design pass lands on: no id keypair custody in the login path (#13409), and SSO never rebinds an id key (#2060).

### 1. Build vs adopt

- **Option A — Hand-build:** build the IdP ourselves on our own components.
- **Option B — Adopt-and-package:** adopt an existing IdP core (e.g. Keycloak-class), package and run it ourselves, fronted by our own PKI.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — adopt-and-package.** Identity protocols are high-risk to hand-roll; our differentiation is the PKI and the integrations, not the protocol code. Note for the design pass: this must be reconciled with Question 0's "separate **minimal** provider" — the fleet CA program's spec already compares Keycloak / Authentik / Kanidm / Zitadel (see Prior work), and the pass must show the adopted core can stay minimal (Drew-only gate, #1253 role claims, PKI-issued signing keys) rather than assuming it.

### 2. Where it runs

- **Option A — Laptop-hosted only:** run the provider as a service on the laptop.
- **Option B — A fleet surface only:** run the provider on a fleet surface.
- **Option C — Both, laptop primary:** run it laptop-hosted first, with a fleet surface as the same provider's second home / reach path, laptop primary.
- **CHOSEN: Option C — both, laptop primary.** It starts where our execution already lives, without closing off a fleet home when reach needs it. (Open sub-question for the design pass: the hosted/Workers edition line under #9077's relatives is a third home candidate — the pass should address it explicitly rather than this story guessing.)

### 3. How relying parties integrate

- **Option A — Direct per service:** each service is configured directly for OIDC/SAML against the provider.
- **Option B — Via the door Workers:** the existing door Workers act as relying-party proxies in front of services.
- **CHOSEN: Both A and B.** They can coexist — direct config where a service supports it well, door Workers as proxies where a service needs a door in front of it. PR #13488's Commander door is the worked example of B; #9086 is the design home for hosted editions consuming the provider directly (A).

### 4. Signing-key rotation

- **Option A — Manual ceremony:** rotation is a deliberate, manual operator ceremony.
- **Option B — Automated rollover:** automated rollover with overlapping JWKS publication, so old and new keys are both trusted during the changeover.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — automated rollover with overlapping JWKS publication.** Overlap makes rotation routine instead of an outage risk, which is what makes rotating often practical. This is already in #13409's scope ("JWKS + key rotation"); Slice 5 proves it rather than designing it from scratch.

### 5. Relationship to the existing Access / Google SSO wiring

Related, not duplicated here: [#13412 — Google federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13412) and [#13411 — GitHub federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13411) / [#13414 — Microsoft federated login door work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13414) (the federated logins under #9077), [#12417 — Google OAuth client creation task](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/12417) (today's Google client for pm.security.cab), and [#13404 — Desktop Commander front door endpoint](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13404) (the Commander OAuth door).

- **Option A — Rip-and-replace:** remove the existing Access/Google wiring and replace it with this provider in one move.
- **Option B — Stand behind the doors:** keep the existing doors and wiring in place, and make this provider the identity standing behind those doors, taking over from Google as the upstream identity over time.
- **CHOSEN: Option B — stand behind the doors, not a rip-and-replace.** The doors our services already use keep working; what changes is whose identity is behind them. This matches #9077's own shape: GitHub/Google/Microsoft stay as federated logins **into** our provider, gated and linked to one account — Google goes from being the identity to being one door into ours.

## Slice plan — in dependency order

1. **Slice 1 — PKI foundation:** cert-generation tooling + root CA + issuing intermediate. *Executed in parallel by the PKI foundation work, 2026-11-23, alongside the filing of this story.* Builds alongside the fleet-ca program ([#9158 — fleet CA canonical secrets model](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/9158) and its design record above) rather than re-specifying a CA model.
2. **Slice 2 — Signing keys:** signing keys for OIDC (JWKS) and SAML, issued from the PKI — the keys [#13409 — minimal devtoday OIDC provider standup](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13409) already scopes as "JWKS + key rotation", now sourced from our PKI instead of provider-local generation.
3. **Slice 3 — The provider itself:** the provider stood up per #13409 + the #9077 children (#13411 / #13412 / #13414 federated logins, #13415 account linking), publishing OIDC discovery/JWKS — **plus SAML IdP metadata + signing, which is new work with no prior design (see Prior work) and needs its own design slice in the design pass.**
4. **Slice 4 — Per-service integrations:** [#13416 — first consumer proving full loop](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13416) (PM stack) first, the Commander door pattern (PR #13488) for Worker-fronted services, and mcpx as a pointing-at relying party per its authorization-server decision ([#1950 — mcpx OAuth authorization conformance work](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/1950), [#13657 — mcpx public endpoint front door](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13657)) — one per service class first, then the remaining services.
5. **Slice 5 — Rotation + revocation drills:** demonstrate signing-key rotation (overlapping JWKS, per Question 4) and certificate revocation end-to-end, building on the keyset/authorization-log substrate ([#2380 — keyset authorization log identity substrate](https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/2380)) instead of inventing a parallel revocation story.

## Closing note

This issue is the design-mill intake (starter issue) for the identity program, so it can route into a full design pass next. The design pass's first job is reconciliation, not invention: the #9077 decision note, the `binding_id` vs `sub` conflict recorded in the id hosted-edition designs, the build-vs-adopt vs minimal-provider tension in Questions 0–1, and the SAML scope, which has no prior art in the repo.

items.title: feat(cold-store-reaper): v4 — R2 S3 client, backup-supabase, eviction
items.body: ## What Reaper v4 wires the `supabase-backups` R2 bucket into the reaper in both directions: filing its newest dump into the Drive cold store, and evicting bucket objects the cold store provably holds. ### S3 client (stdlib only, in `cold_store.py`) - SigV4-signed ListObjectsV2 (continuation-token pagination), GET, DELETE against the account R2 host; `COLD_STORE_R2_HOST` / `COLD_STORE_S3_BASE` overrides mirror the existing endpoint-override pattern. - Credentials only from `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` (operator materializes from Bitwarden); clear error when absent. - GET verifies the received byte count against Content-Length and retries the whole GET up to 3 attempts on truncation / `IncompleteRead` — a truncated read was observed live through this sandbox's egress proxy. ### `backup-supabase` Lists the bucket, picks the newest backup object by LastModified (`manifest.json` excluded — it's the backup system's index, not a dump), downloads it byte-verified, and files it through the existing `put-backup` machinery as db `supabase`. Point-in-time semantics like `backup-d1`: unchanged content is filed again, and the content sha256 is printed so duplication is visible. ### Eviction (trial bucket) - `evict-scan` (dry-run, never deletes): one verdict per object. **Evictable** requires ALL of: content hash known (content-addressed 64-hex filename stem), manifest state `cold`, membership in a `verified` bundle, LastModified at least `--min-age-days` old (default 14), and not among the `--keep-newest` newest bucket objects (default 3). Other verdicts: `hash-unknown` / `not-in-manifest` / `bundle-unverified` / `too-young` / `kept-newest`. Age is checked before position (a young object always carries one of the newest stamps). - `evict` recomputes the scan; without the literal `--apply` it prints the scan and exits non-zero. With `--apply`, each evictable object is **re-verified against the manifest at deletion time**, then S3-deleted, marked `evicted`, and ledgered (`direction='trash'`, `kind='evict'`, `ref=`). One object's failure never aborts the rest. ### Nightly script `scripts/nightly-backup.sh` gains a guarded step 2: `backup-supabase` runs between `backup-d1` and prune only when both R2 credentials are set; otherwise a one-line skip notice (not an error). Header env docs updated; shellcheck/shfmt clean. The existing nightly-backup cron does **not** materialize R2 credentials today, so the step skips there until the cron body is updated (separate operator action). ### Schema — needs a call-out `objects.state` is **not** free text: the pre-v4 CHECK is `('hot','staging','cold','rehydrating','gone')`, so `'evicted'` required a change. Following the v1.1 ledger `'trash'` precedent: schema **v1.2** adds `'evicted'` to the CHECK, local manifests are migrated in place on first open (table rebuild preserving FK-referencing member rows, covered by a test), and the README documents that **the D1 copy needs the same one-line CHECK change before evicted rows can sync** — until then `sync-manifest` fails on the objects statement with D1's own error text. The ledger was deliberately NOT changed (direction stays `'trash'`, kind `'evict'`). ## Tests Offline, no real R2/Google/Cloudflare calls, no real credentials: a fake S3 HTTP layer in the existing fake-server style (SigV4 capture, 2-object list pages, truncate-once GET mode, DELETE recording). **40 tests pass** (30 prior + 10 new), 1 pre-existing skip (worker decoder, node deps absent): - SigV4 header shape + empty-payload hash; list pagination follows continuation tokens; missing-credentials error. - backup-supabase files the newest non-manifest object; the filed copy is byte-whole despite a truncated first GET (retry verified); manifest-only bucket errors. - Evict-scan verdict matrix hits every reason; scan deletes nothing. - evict without `--apply` exits 1 and deletes nothing; `evict --apply` deletes only fully verified evictable objects, writes the trash/evict ledger rows, sets state `evicted`. - An object flipped non-cold between scan and apply is skipped by the deletion-time re-verification. - Pre-v4 manifest migration admits `'evicted'` and preserves member rows. README documents the S3 env, backup-supabase, the eviction policy + safety rails, the nightly change, and notes the `turso/` backup folder exists with no filing command yet (no Turso export source wired — none invented). --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.
