items.title: cold-store: nightly Turso exports via HTTP APIs
items.body: Adds the Turso stream to the cold store's nightly backup, with no `turso` CLI dependency. **`scripts/export-turso.sh`** (new): discovers databases from the Turso Platform API (`GET /v1/organizations//databases`, items carry `Name`/`Hostname`), mints a per-database auth token (`POST .../databases//auth/tokens`), downloads the SQL dump from each database's own libsql endpoint (`GET https:///dump`) with curl, rebuilds a standalone SQLite file with python3, requires `PRAGMA integrity_check` = ok, gzips -6, and files it via `cold-store put-backup turso`. - Skip contract: `TURSO_PLATFORM_API_TOKEN` unset → prints `turso export: skipped (TURSO_PLATFORM_API_TOKEN not set)` and exits 0 — a missing Turso setup never fails the nightly, and the skip is never silent. - Per-database failure (mint, download, rebuild/integrity, gzip, put-backup) prints a loud line naming the DB, the remaining databases are still attempted, and the script exits non-zero at the end. - Token values (platform or per-database) are never printed. Env seams mirror existing precedent: `TURSO_ORG` (default `dezren39`), `TURSO_API_BASE`, `TURSO_DUMP_BASE`, `COLD_STORE_BIN` (cf. `COLD_STORE_S3_BASE`). **`scripts/nightly-backup.sh`**: the Turso step runs after `backup-supabase` and **before** `prune-backups --apply`, so same-night retention covers the new Turso files. **Tests**: `TestTursoExportScript` (3 tests, fully offline) against a fake Turso HTTP server (ThreadingHTTPServer, the repo's fake style) + a stub `cold-store` executable: both fake DBs filed with integrity-verified .db.gz payloads and no token material in output; missing-token skip line + exit 0 + zero filings; one DB's dump returning 500 still files the other and exits non-zero. Full suite: 58 tests (55 + 3), 1 pre-existing skip. shellcheck + shfmt + prettier + ruff format clean. --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need.

items.body:
Drew's directive (2026-10-31): long-term investigation topic — use "Sable uncensored" as the fallback when an API gives a rejection, instead of the request just failing.

This is an INVESTIGATION topic (long-term, staged), not an implementation order. Deliverable is findings + a recommendation; seating anything needs the findings first.

## Problem

Mainstream APIs reject some legitimate work on content-policy grounds — security research and reverse-engineering tooling are the standing fleet examples, alongside adult/creative and controversial-topic work. Today a rejected request simply fails (or worse, in some ecosystems, repeated edgy work puts the account itself at risk). The fleet has no sanctioned lane for work a provider refuses to touch.

## Candidate: "Sable uncensored" — identity UNVERIFIED at filing

First-pass check on 2026-10-31 found NO model or provider named "Sable" in the models.dev / OpenRouter / OpenCode catalogs, and no clear web hit for an uncensored model by that name. Possibilities: a brand-new or niche service, a model id on a specific aggregator, or a dictation artifact for a sound-alike name.

**Deliverable 1 is a positive identification**: provider, model id, endpoint, context window, pricing, tool-calling support, data/retention terms — or a documented finding that no such service exists, with the closest alternatives ranked instead. Alternatives in scope for that ranking (verify, don't assume): Venice AI uncensored models, Cognitive Computations Dolphin builds, hosted abliterated open-weight builds (e.g. UnboundModels' Qwen3.8-27B uncensored), other OpenAI-compatible low-refusal APIs, and self-hosting an abliterated/Dolphin build on fleet hardware.

## Questions the investigation must answer

1. Identity & viability: what is Sable, who runs it, is it still operating, what does it actually serve (weights/build, context window, max output)?
2. Agent fitness: tool calling, structured output, reasoning quality — can it finish real agent work mid-session, or only single-turn text? At what context size?
3. Trigger design: how does the router know a rejection was censorship (error-class shapes per provider)? The companion opencode issue (cross-linked below) covers the other half — censor rejections must never poison route health. This topic covers what the rejected REQUEST does next: fail over to the uncensored lane for that request only.
4. Scope discipline: the uncensored lane is a rejection-triggered special route, NOT a general pool member and never a default. Roles state requirements (Decision 008); this lane's requirement is "the seated models refused this request on content-policy grounds".
5. Privacy & trust: what work may be sent to a niche provider (data terms, retention, training)? Some censored work is censored precisely because it is sensitive.
6. Cost & limits: pricing, rate limits, and whether a free tier exists (relates to the 2026-10-31 free-models investigation: InferX / OpenCode free / alternatives).
7. Bounds: lawful work only; the lane exists for provider over-refusal on legitimate tasks, documented as such.

## Acceptance criteria

- Findings doc: Sable identified or ruled out with evidence; alternatives compared in a table (context, price, tool calls, data terms, quality notes).
- Recommendation: seat / decline / self-host, with reasons, difficulty, and performance considerations.
- If seat: a design sketch for the rejection-triggered route (trigger classification, per-request failover, telemetry) linked to the companion opencode issue — as a follow-up implementation issue, not built from this one.

Companion: developing-today/opencode issue "content-policy (censor) rejections must not count toward model removal, demotion, or disable in routes" (filed 2026-10-31).

items.body:
## Problem

The Meta (Muse Code High Usage) pool's percentage read rests on `POST https://api.meta.ai/muse-code/key` (`subs_usage`), which Meta's server currently does not populate — and has a proven history of not populating in non-exhausted states too (51 consecutive null probes 2026-10-28→11-02 while the console showed 9%→100%). Determination with full evidence: #3347 comment 6650593668. The key endpoint is a valid subscription-active/tier signal but **cannot be the system of record for percentages**.

The faithful source is the dev.meta.ai portal API (the #1301 exporter's source, retired by #5040 in favour of the key endpoint — that trade should be reversed for percentages).

## Fix: laptop-side portal fetcher for the gatherer

On the existing ~15-min gatherer tick, from the LAPTOP (same egress/device as the session, per the 2026-10-26 console investigation's Phase 1 design):

1. **Cookie capture:** read the `llama_dev_sess` cookie (plus `datr` for the same host) for `dev.meta.ai` from the live Helium profile via CDP (`Storage.getCookies` against the laptop Helium debug port). The session is in the desktop Helium's **default** profile, which currently runs without a debug port — the capture step needs Helium launched/attached with `--remote-debugging-port` (or an equivalent profile-copy launch) at capture time. Cookie value goes directly into the gatherer's secret handling — never into a file, log, or this repo. Expected lifetime ~1 year (captured cookie expiry 2027-10-27); treat 401/`Not authenticated` as failure class `session-expired` → row goes stale-with-reason per the #5719 retention behaviour, never zeros.
   - Note (2026-11-04): the Oct-era profile copy at `~/atlas/helium-chatgpt-profile-copy` no longer authenticates (401 on `/api/auth/me`) — do not reuse it; capture from the live profile.
2. **Reads (cookie-auth GETs, base `https://dev.meta.ai`, team `1073226932208501` = "My Team"):**
   - `GET /api/portal/teams/{team_id}/subscription-quota` → `{subscription_quota: {tier: "Muse Code High Usage", as_of, window_weighted_used, window_weighted_limit: "100000000000", window_duration_secs: 18000, window_resets_at, weekly_weighted_used, weekly_weighted_limit: "300000000000", weekly_resets_at}}` — used/limit are stringified integers in weighted units; % = used/limit; the 18000s window is the rolling window, plus the weekly window. Proven live payload 2026-10-27 (window 1.02%, weekly 8.83%; resets matched the key endpoint's boundaries exactly).
   - `GET /api/portal/teams/{team_id}/billing-banner` → `{kind, remaining_minor_units, currency}` — free credits remaining (minor units = cents; $148.57 at last read).
   - Map into the existing meta row shape (`meta:high-usage`): rolling + weekly windows with usedPercent + resetsAt, free credits as the balance figure. The portal's own note applies: "new usage can take up to an hour to appear" — carry `as_of` as measuredAt.
3. **Keep the key-endpoint fetcher as a cross-check**, not the source: its `is_subs_active` / `subs_tier_name` / `require_payment` remain the cheapest active/tier signal, and an inference-path 429 (quota exhausted, with reset) corroborates a 100% weekly. If portal and key-endpoint disagree about exhaustion, prefer the portal's percentages and record the disagreement in the row's reason.
4. **Testing:** fixture tests from the captured 2026-10-27 payload shape (stringified weighted units, % derivation, reset mapping) + the session-expired and portal-error classes; oracle = the recorded payload + a live console read at verification time.

## Acceptance

- [ ] Two consecutive gatherer ticks carry a fresh ok meta entry with real (non-null) rolling + weekly percentages sourced from the portal API.
- [ ] The laptop live route (`/api/quota/meta`) and the hub entry agree.
- [ ] A forced session-expired test (bad cookie) yields the `session-expired` stale-with-reason row, not zeros and not a silent null.
- [ ] #3347's remaining acceptance (recovered read recorded in the pool-change ledger by the next steward pass) can be satisfied.

Related: #3347 (root-cause determination), #1301 (original exporter, closed), #5040 (source switch being partially reversed), #5719 (retention behaviour), #5101 (board stale-fallback display).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The gatherer's Meta percentage read comes from the dev.meta.ai portal API (`subscription-quota`) fetched laptop-side on the existing gatherer tick; both the rolling (18000s) and weekly window percentages are computed from used/limit.
- [ ] The cookie is captured from the live Helium profile at capture time and passes only through the gatherer's secret handling — it appears in no file, log, or repo content.
- [ ] A 401 / `Not authenticated` response is failure class `session-expired`: the row goes stale-with-reason per #5719 retention, never zeros.
- [ ] The key endpoint remains only as a subscription-active/tier signal; it is no longer the system of record for percentages.

items.title: github-backup(queue): retained failed events starve polling — /queue returns only the first 500 events with no pagination

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

items.body:
## Finding (from PR review)

Codex P2 on PR #3290 (chatgpt-codex-connector[bot], 2026-11-01T02:00:06Z): "Allow queue polling to progress past retained failed events" — https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/3290#discussion_r4434070386

> If the queue contains 500 older events for unavailable planned mirrors, retaining those events now prevents later events for healthy repositories from being processed. The Worker in `infra/github-backup/worker/src/index.js:55-61` returns only the first 500 entries and neither follows nor exposes a pagination cursor, so every drain retries the same failed batch until recovery or expiration of the seven-day TTL. I reproduced this with 500 missing-mirror events followed by one healthy-repository event: repeated drains never attempted the healthy repository. Preserve failed events, but add pagination or another mechanism that allows polling to advance past them.

Context: PR #3290 itself introduced the retain-on-failure ack discipline (an event is acked only after a successful fetch), which is what makes retained events accumulate at the head of the queue.

## No-response evidence

- PR #3290 merged with the finding unaddressed: the inline comment has no replies, and GraphQL `reviewThreads` for PR #3290 shows its sole thread `isResolved=false`.
- No fix commit after the comment: the 500-entry cap with no cursor is still present on current main (below).

## Still-live evidence (verified this run, current main)

- `infra/github-backup/worker/src/index.js`, `GET /queue` handler: `const list = await env.GHB_EVENTS.list({ prefix: "ev:", limit: 500 });` — it iterates only `list.keys`, never follows `list.cursor` / `list_complete`, and the response exposes no cursor to the drainer.
- `infra/github-backup/bin/drain_queue.py` polls that endpoint once per run and processes only the returned `events`; retained failed events (acked only on a successful fetch, per the #3219 discipline documented in its header) therefore re-occupy the same first-500 window on every drain until their mirrors recover or the 7-day KV TTL expires.

## Dedupe

Searched open and closed issues for "drain queue 500 pagination" and "github-backup queue polling retained" (2026-11-01): no issue covers this.

## Acceptance criteria

- Queue polling can progress past 500 retained events: the Worker follows the KV list cursor (or exposes pagination) and the drainer can reach events beyond the first 500.
- Failed events are still preserved (the retain-on-failure ack discipline is not weakened).
- A regression test/repro with >500 retained failed events followed by a healthy-repo event shows the healthy event being processed.
- Or the finding is resolved by a documented decision on this issue.

items.title: cold-store: atlas Turso export fails to rebuild (duplicate chunk_id in vec table dump)
items.body:
## Problem

`cold-store-nightly` on the laptop (device amd) has failed its `export-turso` step on Nov 17 and Nov 18, so the nightly run reports `FAILED steps: export-turso`. Every Turso database exports except the large `atlas` database:

- Nov 17 03:26 CST: `turso export: ERROR: atlas: dump download failed` (the `/dump` download for `atlas`).
- Nov 18 04:19 and 05:11 CST: `Error near line 458145: UNIQUE constraint failed: vec_snowflake_m_v2_768_f32.chunk_id`, then `turso export: ERROR: atlas: dump did not rebuild into a SQLite file`. Both attempts fail on the same dump line.

The Nov 18 prune listing keeps no `atlas` export at all, so this database has no cold-store copy in the retained set. All other databases (the `atlas-core-*` shards, `fleet-mirror`, `muse-meta`, `notes-submissions`) filed normally.

## What is known

- `vec_snowflake_m_v2_768_f32` is a plain table with `chunk_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY` in the repo's fixtures. A primary-key collision on rebuild means the `/dump` text carries the same `chunk_id` twice. That fits a dump paginated over a table that was being written during the dump, or a schema on the live `atlas` database that differs from the fixtures. It has not been confirmed.
- `export-turso.sh` deletes its work dir on exit, so the failing dump is not kept for inspection.

## Ask

1. Keep the failing dump (or at least the table name, the duplicated `chunk_id` and how many dump lines carry it) when the rebuild fails, so the cause can be read off the next run.
2. Fix the cause: a consistent dump for `atlas`, or a rebuild that tolerates a key repeated by a non-snapshot dump only where the repeated rows are identical. Do not drop rows silently.
3. Acceptance: one nightly run files an `atlas` export that passes the existing integrity and user-table checks.

Found while checking laptop backups for #10296. Related: #1391 (dump repair filter).

items.title: design: secrets plane — delta refresh, broker peer sync, dual-store puts
items.body:
# Design: secrets plane — delta refresh, broker peer sync, dual-store puts

Direction: Drew, 2026-11-23 ~19:12 CST. Extends #13893 (cold-refresh batching + client fallback bound) and #13894 (broker performance under load). Where this design and #13893's batching-only proposal overlap, **this design supersedes the batching-only framing**: the one-call list becomes the full-refresh mechanism *inside* a delta-first design, not the end state. #13893's client-wait bound survives unchanged (Slice 1 below). #13894 remains the performance-tracking issue; this design addresses its cold-refresh row and part of the client pile-up cause.

Related, not duplicated: #10358 (secrets scoping — prefix / vault / store selection decides *which* store and namespace a name resolves to; this design decides *how* brokers and stores stay in sync), #9158 (canonical secrets model, provider adapters & custody policy), #13081 (heal cadence starving refresh — fixed), #5504 (partial refresh evicting cached secrets — its failure mode is a correctness constraint on Slice 2).

## 1. Problem and evidence

The sandbox secrets broker refreshes by shelling out to `bws secret get <id>` **once per secret** — 242 spawns, ~160–220s cold (measured 2026-11-23, #13893). Refresh runs at startup and every 900s. During that window the broker is present-but-not-serving, and clients hang instead of falling back (>120s observed, #13893), so every sandbox restart wedges every secrets consumer for minutes. The estate has two brokers (sandbox + laptop) holding the same set with no way to learn from each other: if the laptop broker refreshed a minute ago, the sandbox broker still pays the full upstream cost. Writes are worse: `fleet secrets` is read-only today (verified, §3), so a new secret is minted out-of-band in one store and propagates only when a refresh happens to notice it (#6275's read-through gap is the same shape).

## 2. Goals and non-goals

**Goals**

1. A broker restart reaches `serving` in seconds in the normal case (peer up), and in one upstream list call in the worst case (peer down, no cache).
2. Refresh cost tracks *change*, not set size: pull only secrets whose revision moved since the last refresh.
3. Brokers prove sync with a set hash; equal hashes mean synced, full stop.
4. `fleet secrets` gains a write path (`put`) and explicit cache controls (`refresh`, `--upstream`, `--no-cache`), with puts propagated so no peer or store has to re-fetch to converge.
5. Both stores (Bitwarden Secrets + 1Password) are kept in sync by construction, with one designated primary so sync direction is never ambiguous.

**Non-goals**

- Namespaces / per-device store selection — that is #10358; v1 syncs the whole set, per Drew's explicit simplification ("for broker-to-broker, it might just be simpler to just send everything it has from one location to the other… we can pull that back at that point").
- Replacing either store, or embedding them in the fleet binary — filed as separate future-work to-dos, cross-linked below.
- A new trust root or enrollment system — peer trust is the fleet enrollment/broker trust already in place.

## 3. Verified premises

Verified by the filing lane 2026-11-24; anything not verified live is marked.

- **`fleet secrets` today has exactly two verbs, `get` and `list`, and is read-only** — verified from the installed binary's help (`Commands: get, list`). `refresh` and `put` are new surface.
- **`bws secret list <project>` returns the whole set in one call, including values and a per-secret `revisionDate`** — verified live against the estate's Bitwarden project (bws 2.1.0): 244 secrets, fields `creationDate, id, key, note, organizationId, projectId, revisionDate, value` (count and field names only were inspected; no values). So both batching and delta-by-`revisionDate` are supported by the CLI *today*; the broker simply doesn't use the list call.
- **bws write verbs exist** (`bws secret create / edit / delete`) — verified from CLI surface and existing estate scripts.
- **1Password CLI (`op` 2.41.0) is installed** in the sandbox recovery bin and on the laptop — verified. `op item create` / `op item edit` exist (help verified). `op service-account ratelimit` exists (help verified) — service-account rate limits are a real, queryable constraint, not a theoretical one.
- **NOT live-verified:** `op item list --format json` field shape. Documented behaviour is that items carry `created_at` / `updated_at`, and list returns metadata (values need a per-item `op item get`). The laptop's `op` has no account configured in a plain SSH shell ("No accounts configured for use with 1Password CLI"), so this lane did not read a live item. Slice 5 includes a capability spike to verify before the mirror-write path is built on it.
- **Peer channel exists**: the tiered broker shape (local → laptop → in-process) and its tokens (by name: `fleet.secrets-broker-token`, `fleet.queue-broker-token`, `fleet.laptop-agent-token`) are live; sandbox↔laptop traffic rides the tailnet (DERP-relayed at 490–873ms RTT per #13894, still WireGuard-encrypted end to end).

## 4. Alternatives considered

**A. Batching only (#13893 as filed).** One `bws secret list` per refresh replaces 242 gets. Cold refresh drops from ~3–4 min to seconds. Honest tradeoff: refresh cost still scales with set size, brokers still can't learn from each other, no write path, no sync proof. Necessary but not sufficient — absorbed as the full-refresh mechanism in the chosen shape.

**B. Delta refresh from the upstream store only (no peer sync).** Refresh = list, filter `revisionDate > watermark`, apply changes. Cheapest correct refresh, but a restarted sandbox broker with an empty cache still needs a full set from upstream, and two brokers can hold different sets between refreshes with no way to know. Rejected as the end state; it is the upstream half of the chosen shape.

**C. Full-set broker-to-broker transfer on every sync.** Drew's allowed v1 simplification taken literally for *every* cycle: brokers just send each other everything. Simple and obviously correct; at ~244 small secrets the payload is trivial today. Tradeoff: it re-sends everything forever and gives no cheap "are we synced?" answer. The chosen shape keeps full-set transfer as the v1 *peer payload* but gates it behind the set hash, so the common case is one hash comparison and transfers happen only on real divergence.

**D. Store-level replication only (no broker protocol).** Brokers stay dumb caches; Bitwarden and 1Password are synced by a separate replicator. Rejected: it does nothing for the restart wedge (the actual incident), and broker-to-broker is where the latency pain lives.

## 5. Chosen approach

### 5.1 Delta refresh (upstream leg)

Each broker keeps a durable watermark: the start time of its last successful refresh, minus a small skew overlap (Drew's "from maybe just before the last refresh started"). A refresh is one `bws secret list` call; entries with `revisionDate` after the watermark are applied, ids absent from the list are deleted locally, everything else is untouched. The list call carries values, so a delta refresh and a full refresh are the same call with different apply rules — there is no per-secret fetch path left. A failed or partial list applies **nothing** (the #5504 lesson: a partial refresh must never evict).

### 5.2 Broker-to-broker peer sync

On startup and on each refresh tick, a broker asks its trusted peer for `{set_hash, last_upstream_refresh_at, count}`:

- Hashes equal → synced; done. This is the steady state and costs one round trip.
- Peer refreshed from upstream more recently than local, hashes differ → pull the peer's full set (v1 payload = everything, per Drew's simplification) and adopt it, recording the peer as the source and the peer's watermark as the local watermark.
- Peer down or stale → fall back to the upstream delta/full refresh (§5.1).

Consequence, as Drew specified: a sandbox broker needs a full upstream refresh **only if the laptop is down AND it restarted with no cache**. Namespaces and selective pull-back are deferred until requirements actually diverge.

### 5.3 Set hash

The sync proof is a hash over the whole set: sort by name, hash each `(name, value)` pair, combine. Because a bare hash of a low-entropy value is guessable offline, pair hashes are **keyed** (HMAC with the peer token) and the set hash is exchanged only between authenticated brokers, never logged in full (truncated in logs) and never published. Equal keyed hashes from two brokers that share the peer key prove the sets are identical without either side sending values.

### 5.4 Client surface

- `fleet secrets get <name>` — unchanged default path (local broker → laptop → in-process).
- `fleet secrets get <name> --upstream` — resolve from the upstream peer/store, bypassing the local cache.
- `fleet secrets get <name> --no-cache` — bypass all broker caches; straight to the primary store.
- `fleet secrets refresh` — force the local broker through §5.2/§5.1 now instead of at the next tick; reports which leg served it (peer / upstream-delta / upstream-full) and the resulting set hash.
- `fleet secrets put <name>` — new; §5.5. (Value via stdin/prompt, never argv, so it stays out of shell history and process lists.)
- The #13893 client bound rides along: a non-serving local broker is a cache miss within ~2–5s, never a hang.

### 5.5 Put semantics (chosen default)

**Default: the put is written by the node that receives it to the primary store first; that write is the commit point. The writer then pushes the value directly to its peer broker and writes the mirror store; the peer never re-fetches.** Drew offered both shapes (send-upstream-and-let-upstream-write, or write-and-push); write-first-then-push is chosen because (a) the primary store is the source of truth, so the commit must land there before any cache holds the value — otherwise a crash between push and store-write leaves caches holding a secret the truth doesn't have; (b) a node holding only one store still works: it sends the put upstream to the laptop (which always has both), and the laptop performs the dual write — that is the send-upstream shape, kept exactly where it's needed, as the escalation path rather than the default. Mirror-store or peer-push failure after the primary commit does not fail the put; it queues a reconcile (§5.6) and the put reports `committed, propagation pending`.

### 5.6 Dual-store sync and the primary designation

**Recommendation: Bitwarden Secrets is the primary; 1Password is the fallback/mirror.** Drew's initial lean was 1Password primary "if that helps", with the reverse explicitly acceptable if better supported. The evidence supports the reverse:

- The entire running broker stack already authenticates to Bitwarden with machine access tokens, headless, today. 1Password on the laptop has no account configured outside its desktop/service-account setup (§3).
- Bitwarden's one list call returns values *and* `revisionDate` — it is the only store that can serve as the delta source. 1Password's list returns metadata only; a full pull is one call per item.
- 1Password service accounts carry rate limits (the CLI ships a `ratelimit` verb to inspect them); a chatty sync loop against 1Password as primary would spend that budget on bookkeeping. As mirror, it receives one write per put — well inside any limit.
- 1Password's strength in this estate is human-side custody and escrow (the IdP CA material is already escrowed there). As mirror/fallback it keeps that role: if Bitwarden is down, brokers serve from cache and 1Password is the human recovery path; reads can fall back to it, writes queue until the primary returns (or Drew rules an emergency promotion).

Sync direction is therefore never ambiguous: primary → mirror, primary → brokers, broker → broker (§5.2). A periodic reconcile compares the primary's set hash against each broker's and (via item metadata) the mirror's, and repairs drift from the primary, logging names only. The only bootstrap case where a node lacks both stores is a node with just the Bitwarden CLI: it uses the canonical Bitwarden path — acquire its access token via the existing bootstrap route (the token is itself a vaulted secret, fetched by name) — and from then on it is a primary-capable node. Per Drew: the only time a node doesn't bootstrap to having both stores reachable is if the canonical path doesn't have the secret or the CLI isn't installed.

## 6. Security analysis

- **Peer trust**: broker-to-broker sync introduces no new trust. Peers authenticate with the existing broker tokens under the existing fleet enrollment; a non-enrolled party cannot request a set, a hash, or a push. Put (§5.5) requires the same enrollment-grade auth as other broker admin surface — it is a write into the estate's secret store and is treated that way.
- **Values in transit**: values move only on (a) the existing broker channel over the tailnet (WireGuard-encrypted; DERP relays see ciphertext, #13894), and (b) broker↔store TLS. No new plaintext path is created. Full-set peer transfer (v1) widens *how much* value material crosses the peer channel per sync, which is why it is gated behind hash divergence instead of running every tick.
- **Hash leakage**: pair hashes are keyed (§5.3) so a leaked set hash does not enable offline guessing of low-entropy values; hashes are truncated in logs.
- **Logging**: names, counts, timings, truncated hashes, and the serving leg — never values, never full hashes, never tokens. Put audit records name + actor + timestamp only.
- **Deletion**: a delete in the primary propagates as a set-diff deletion (§5.1/§5.2); peer adoption is wholesale-set replacement from the more-recently-refreshed side, so a deleted secret cannot be resurrected by a stale peer — the peer's older watermark loses by rule.

## 7. Build slices (dependency-ordered)

**S1 — Client bound + one-call refresh (the surviving #13893 fixes).** Broker refresh uses one `bws secret list`; clients fall through a non-serving local broker within ~2–5s. *Acceptance:* cold refresh measured in seconds on the live set; a `fleet secrets get` issued during a refresh returns from the laptop tier or errors promptly, never hangs >5s; #13893 closes on this slice's evidence.

**S2 — Delta refresh + watermark.** Durable watermark with skew overlap; apply-only-changed; deletion by id-set diff; partial list applies nothing. *Acceptance:* with exactly one secret changed upstream, refresh applies one entry (log shows names/counts) and the set hash moves; with none changed, refresh is a no-op beyond the list call; a killed mid-refresh broker restarts into the pre-refresh set (no eviction, #5504 regression test).

**S3 — Set hash + peer status.** Keyed set hash (§5.3); brokers expose `{set_hash, last_upstream_refresh_at, count}` to authenticated peers. *Acceptance:* two brokers holding the same set report equal hashes; changing one value on one side flips only that side's hash; unauthenticated hash requests are refused.

**S4 — Peer pull sync.** §5.2 logic on startup and tick; full-set peer payload; upstream fallback. *Acceptance:* sandbox broker cold start with the laptop peer up reaches `serving` with **zero** bws invocations (proven by bws-call logging); cold start with the peer down still reaches `serving` via upstream; a secret changed on the laptop converges to the sandbox on the next tick without either side calling upstream.

**S5 — Client surface: `refresh`, `get --upstream/--no-cache`, `put`.** §5.4/§5.5 semantics, including the one-store-node escalation to the laptop for dual write. Includes the 1Password capability spike (verify §3's unverified premise) before the mirror write is built. *Acceptance:* a put from the sandbox is readable from the laptop broker and present in both stores without waiting for a refresh tick; a put from a Bitwarden-only node lands in both stores via the laptop; `refresh` reports its serving leg; put audit log contains the name and actor and no value.

**S6 — Reconcile + drift repair.** Periodic primary↔broker↔mirror hash comparison; repair from primary; alert on persistent drift. *Acceptance:* a hand-edited mirror entry is detected and restored on the next reconcile, logged by name only; a hand-edited broker cache entry is likewise repaired from the primary; two consecutive failed reconciles raise an alert through the existing PM path.

## 8. Rollout and rollback

Roll out per slice, laptop broker first, sandbox second (the laptop is the estate's always-has-both node and the natural first peer). S1–S2 are broker-internal and roll back by binary revert to the previous published fleet build. S3–S4 add peer verbs behind a config flag defaulting to off until both sides run the new build; disabling the flag returns both brokers to independent upstream refresh (today's behaviour). S5's `put` ships dark (verb present, disabled by config) until S6's reconcile is live, so no write path exists before drift repair does. The stores themselves are never migrated — Bitwarden already holds the set; 1Password mirror population is a one-time copy *from* the primary, verified by hash before S5 enables mirror writes.

## 9. Verification plan

- **Timed cold-start, peer up:** restart the sandbox broker with an empty cache; measure time to `serving`; assert zero bws calls (S4).
- **Timed cold-start, peer down:** stop the laptop broker, restart the sandbox broker empty; it must still reach `serving` via upstream — the one case Drew named where a full upstream refresh is expected — and the elapsed time is recorded against the S1 baseline (one list call, seconds, vs today's ~160–220s).
- **Hash proof:** force a one-value divergence; hashes differ; run sync; hashes equal; sets byte-identical by name+value comparison inside the test harness (values never printed).
- **Put propagation:** put from each node class (dual-store laptop, Bitwarden-only sandbox); verify presence in both stores and both brokers, and timing.
- **Drift drill:** hand-edit the mirror and a broker cache; reconcile repairs both, logs names only.
- **Log audit:** grep all new log paths for a canary value planted via put; it must appear nowhere.

## 10. Open questions (named deciders)

1. **Primary designation** — this design recommends Bitwarden primary / 1Password mirror (§5.6) against Drew's initial lean, on the evidence in §3. **Decider: Drew** (ratify or reverse; the design's mechanics are unchanged if reversed, but the delta source moves and S2/S5 get harder — §5.6 says why).
2. **Put availability** — should `put` work from any enrolled node at S5, or laptop-only until S6 proves reconcile? **Decider: Drew** (security posture call).
3. **Peer protocol home** — extend the secrets broker's own HTTP surface, or carry sync on the queue-broker channel? **Decider: fleet design owner (Archer)**, settled at S3 from the existing broker code, not by preference.
4. **1Password write identity** — service account vs desktop-integration session for the mirror write. **Decider: Archer**, after the S5 capability spike (the laptop CLI currently has no configured account in a plain shell).
5. **Token-generation command name** for the `fleet init` bootstrap to-do (companion issue) — Drew left the name undecided ("I don't know, `fleet generate a net`" was thinking aloud). **Decider: Drew**, when that to-do is picked up.

## 11. Companion to-dos (filed alongside, future work)

- **Embed both stores in the fleet binary** — a configurable feature embedding 1Password + Bitwarden Secrets access directly into `fleet`, so a node downloads one binary and has everything it needs. (Issue link added in a comment below.)
- **`fleet init` bootstrap command** — the one-time-token bootstrap (token redeemed at a generic URL) as a fleet command, plus a token-generation command that talks to the Cloudflare worker and returns a one-time token a service can hand to a new server. (Issue link added in a comment below.)

*Filed by the SECRETS-PLANE-DESIGN lane, 2026-11-24. Secrets are referenced by name only throughout; no values appear in this issue.*

# Open-PR clearance programme 2026-11-24: every open PR merged, fixed+merged, or tasked

Ordered by Drew, 2026-11-24 01:08 CST: "review every open pr and merge or fix and merge or open a priority task, each should have one or more related issues and one or more queue items. open prs need to be handled. increase priority if item isn't being worked. if item is blocked then prioritize the blockers in order until everything to unlock is escalated with the open pr item next. aggressively review any questions consider if it's a real blocker if it can be handled. if there's truly no way around it consider splitting out the blocked parts if this will unblock children, handle and prioritize the items that can be worked and increase question priority for the split out part(s). you can always split issues, add research/fix issues, or whatever is needed. do whatever is needed to make things move. be aggressive and decisive."

## Relationship to the queue programme

Sibling programme to #14158 (queue reprioritization programme 2026-11-24). This programme's outcomes feed #14158's pass-3 band audit: every task created here enters the queue under the same priority law, and blocker-chain escalations here are inputs to its reorder.

## Scope

Every open PR in every repo Drew owns/admins. Opening snapshot (search API, 2026-11-24 ~07:10Z): dezren39 388, developing-today 174 (of which this repo 118), developing-today-forks 32, plus the long-tail orgs — full census lands as the first record on this issue. PRs in repos Drew does NOT own are listed separately and not merged.

## Per-PR outcomes (exactly one each)

1. **Merge** — verified ready: diff reviewed, no unresolved conflict, does what its issue says. CI runs on main only; verification is diff + linked-issue acceptance + warranted checks. Never force-push main.
2. **Fix and merge** — small mechanical gap (conflict rebase, stale branch, trivial failing piece) fixed in a worktree via the standard routes, then merged.
3. **Priority queue task** — real work remains: a packet naming the PR, its issue(s), what blocks it, and the fix scope, at a priority set by the rules below.

Tracking completeness: every PR ends with one or more related issues AND one or more queue items. Orphan PRs are created/linked into both.

## Priority rules (named scale only; higher number = lower priority)

immediate 5 / now 10 / critical 20 / urgent 30 / very high 40 / high 50 / medium 60 / low 70 / very low 80 / minimal 90.

- An item that isn't being worked gets its priority increased (number lowered).
- A blocked item: its blocker chain is prioritized in order — everything needed to unlock is escalated, with the PR's own item next behind its last blocker.
- Questions are reviewed aggressively: a question answerable from Drew's recorded decisions or standing statements is answered, not left waiting. A truly immovable blocker is SPLIT OUT into its own issue/task (its question priority raised); everything that can move is handled and prioritized now.

## Hard rails

- PRs #13234 and #13237 are recorded hard skips — held, never merged or modified.
- #14158's held list (hard-skip issues, `user/*` labels, task 18533) stays untouched.
- A PR with a live claim by a working lane is reviewed and routed (task/priority/notes), never stomped.
- Secrets by name only. Every merge, fix, task, split, and priority change is recorded with evidence on this issue; a change that cannot be verified by read-back did not happen.

Progress records land as comments on this issue at each batch boundary.

items.body:
# infra: repo-queue PostgREST `timeout: global` failures are lane-visible again — recurrence after #6450 closed (2026-11-06 ~21:15–21:31Z)

## Evidence (lane code-w shift, 2026-11-06)

Five consecutive `fleet queue` calls failed with the same signature, exit 4:

- `fleet queue health --queue repo-health-code-pilot` — failed ~21:15Z, ~21:17Z, ~21:20Z, ~21:31Z (4 attempts)
- `fleet queue claim --queue repo-health-code-pilot --worker repo-worker-code --lane code-w --lease-seconds 2700` — failed ~21:24Z (1 attempt)

Every call: stderr `repo-queue: PostgREST request failed: timeout: global`, exit 4, each taking ~90s before failing. No task could be claimed; the lane-W shift ended with zero tasks worked. No claim was recorded by the failed claim call as far as the client can tell (the verb errored; atomic claim semantics + the 57014 rollback rationale in #6450 say a timed-out write rolled back — worth a broker-side confirm).

## Why this is a recurrence, not #6450 itself

#6450 closed COMPLETED 2026-11-06T17:44:35Z after PR #6584 deployed the posture (broker health cache 12s TTL, paced enqueues, shared backoff base 500ms ×2 cap 20s ×6 attempts on 57014/PGRST002). Its closing note recorded that in the post-deployment window (~17:48–17:51Z) timeouts still occurred at the DB but **no queue verb surfaced a failure** — calls were slow (~50s worst) but succeeded. Its close rule: the issue closes when a captured failure window proves the root cause, or the posture eliminates the windows.

This window breaks that: verbs are surfacing failures again, repeatedly, over 15+ minutes — either a longer/deeper window than backoff can absorb, a different failing leg (health aggregation was already the expensive verb: one `repo_queue_health` read cost 6,315 ms in the #6450 capture), or the sandbox client vintage (the #6450 note said installed client binaries update at the next fleet install/switch — the client-side backoff may not be live on this sandbox yet).

## Pointers

- Standing capture from #6450 arm (a): cron `queue-capture-6450` + broker failure-events log (`~/.local/state/queue-broker/failure-events.jsonl`) should have this window — check `hidden_files/queue-capture-6450/captures/` for a failure capture covering 21:15–21:31Z and correlate the pg_stat delta.
- Related but distinct: #6616 (backoff `is_retryable` substring-matching can misclassify permanent errors as statement timeouts).
- Prior occurrences: #6450 (2026-11-06, closed), #5370 (2026-11-04, closed).

## Acceptance

- The 21:15–21:31Z window is attributed from the capture stream (failing verb + DB-side cause), or a broker/client fix ships that makes this window class non-lane-visible, with the verification recorded here.
- Confirm no orphan claim was left by the failed 21:24Z claim call (task claimed by repo-worker-code / lane code-w with no checkpoint would be the tell).

items.body:
**DRAFT design — filed for Drew's ratification under the design-protection rule (2026-11-11): this stays open until Drew parks or abandons it. Wording below is a draft in the fleet's voice, not Drew's.**

## Drew's ask (2026-11-12 ~01:43 CST, main chat)

> "keep a list of all orgs in hatch personal and the permissions and apps each that you can refer back to, or maybe a table in turso and wire a fleet subcommand to list whatever"

Context: the fleet GitHub Apps parity + coverage program (epic to be linked below) put all three fleet Apps — `developing-today`, `developing-today-fleet`, `developing-today-backup` — at one identical nine-permission set across all 102 orgs Drew admins. The first deliverable is a committed registry document in dezren39/hatch-personal (seed data for this issue). This issue is the durable upgrade Drew sketched: the registry as queryable data, not a document that goes stale.

## Proposal

1. **Turso tables** for the registry: orgs (login, Drew's role, repo counts, verified-at), apps (slug, app id, owner, permission set, events), installations (app × account, installation id, repository selection, permissions as installed, verified-at).
2. **Sync path**: a fleet job that regenerates the tables from GitHub ground truth. Ground-truth rule learned 2026-11-12: each App's own JWT against `GET /app/installations` (fully paginated) is authoritative. `GET /orgs/<org>/installations` under an OAuth token produced false negatives (33 orgs wrongly reported as having no fleet Apps) and must not be used for coverage claims.
3. **`fleet orgs list` subcommand**: prints the registry (org → role → repos → per-App install state + permission set), with a `--drift` mode that re-reads GitHub and flags any installation whose permissions differ from the App's current set (the acceptance-pending state this program just swept).

## Acceptance criteria

- `fleet orgs list` prints all 104 memberships with role, repo counts, and per-App state matching the hatch-personal registry doc.
- Drift mode exits non-zero and names the installation when any App installation's permissions differ from that App's declared set.
- Sync runs from the App JWTs; no OAuth-token coverage claims anywhere in the path.
- The registry doc in hatch-personal links here as the living successor; this issue stays open until Drew ratifies, parks, or abandons the design.

Program home: the fleet GitHub Apps epic (linked in comments). Related: #8805 (design-register epic — this program grew out of its token audit).

items.body:
## What this is

#alignment (C0CBYQR65LL) is the agent coordination channel. Aster is in it and proposed the channel contract on 2026-10-28 (verified senders; every dispatch carries ID/owner/scope/evidence; ACK/BLOCKED then RESULT in-thread; dedupe; no credentials). OpenClaw is not in it yet — its bot binding and delivery are unverified. Drew asked 2026-10-29 to add OpenClaw and to settle whether one channel for all agents is enough, or each pair needs its own point-to-point path.

## The topology question

**One shared channel** (recommended):
- Channels stay O(1) as agents are added; pairwise grows O(n^2).
- Every dispatch and result sits in one record — the OpenClaw/OpenCode review needs to see traffic it was not part of.
- Threads per dispatch keep it readable; the contract keeps it disciplined.

**Point-to-point per pair**:
- Wins only for high-volume pair traffic, or content that should not be visible to the other agents.
- Costs: fragmented record, hidden context, and N^2 channels to babysit as the roster grows (Muse, Aster, OpenClaw, OpenCode today; more coming).

Recommendation: one shared #alignment for all dispatch and results, one thread per dispatch ID, contract as Aster proposed. Add a point-to-point path only when a specific pair proves it needs one (volume or sensitivity), and record that exception here.

## Work

1. Bind the OpenClaw bot into #alignment; verify send and receive both ways with a harmless round-trip.
2. Publish the sender ID registry (Muse, Aster, OpenClaw) in the channel and on this issue.
3. Adopt the contract for all agents; the first OpenClaw dispatch follows it.

## Acceptance

- OpenClaw posts and replies in #alignment, verified both directions.
- Topology decision recorded (Drew) and the contract pinned/linked.

items.title: Connection perf: coalesce queue claim flow to 1 round trip, cross-service batch, real file-transfer verb
items.body:
## Coalesce queue claim flow + add a real file-transfer verb (fewer round trips, WS-C census)

Part of epic #5412. Census evidence: WS-C comment on #5701 (2026-11-04). Every sandbox↔laptop round trip costs ~200–600 ms warm, so round-trip COUNT is the lever until/unless the multiplexed-tunnel work lands.

### Round-trip census today (code + logs)
| Operation | Transport round trips | Wall (measured) |
|---|---|---|
| Single trivial exec (`laptop-agent.py exec -- true`) | 1 (unix to session proxy + 1 pooled-tunnel HTTP request) | wall 346–719 ms; trip p50 369 ms |
| `fleet queue claim` (one claim) | 1 (`call("/claim")` → one `broker_roundtrip` → one `unix_roundtrip`; repo-queue crate `crates/repo-queue/src/main.rs` cmd_claim/call) | ~1 trip ≈ 0.3–0.6 s warm |
| Claimant launch flow (claim + lane + bind) | 3 separate CLI invocations = 3 round trips (cmd_lane, cmd_bind are separate `call()`s) | ~1–2 s warm, ×3 failure surfaces |
| Detached job to completion (`run` + `poll` loop) | 1 + N polls (poll sleeps 3 s client-side and re-requests per iteration, laptop-agent.py `poll`) | grows with job length |
| Small file fetch from laptop | NO file verb exists: fetch = 1 exec round trip with `base64 -w0` in a shell string (measured 301 ms wall for /etc/hostname), 1 MiB/stream cap, +33% base64 size, no resume/offsets | 1 trip + encoding overhead |

Also measured: `fleet queue health` took 2.1 s and 5.8 s in two live probes (vs 0.30 s in the #5701 stage-2 window) — it visibly resolves secrets ("resolved via bitwarden") plus queries, i.e. multiple internal round trips; health should be 1 lightweight trip.

### Proposal
1. **Batch endpoint for the claim flow**: queue-broker `POST /claim-flow` {queue, worker, lane, session, launched_by} performing claim+lane+bind server-side (laptop-local, Supabase calls stay on the laptop) and returning the bound row. Client `fleet queue claim --bind ...` uses it when session info is present; the 3 separate verbs remain for compatibility. 3 trips → 1.
2. **Generic batch already half-exists**: the daemon `/exec` accepts `cmds: [...]` (exec-batch measured: 10 trivial commands in ONE trip, 483 ms wall total vs ~400 ms EACH singly). Publish this pattern to queue/secrets clients: a `/batch` on the session-proxy protocol that carries several service requests (mixed ports) in one frame and fans out at the broker. Client libraries coalesce independent calls made in one invocation.
3. **File-transfer verb**: daemon `GET /file?path=&off=&len=` returning raw bytes (Content-Type application/octet-stream, byte-range via query — the jobs poll already proves the offset pattern) + client `laptop-agent.py fetch PATH OUT`. No base64, chunked by offset, resume = re-request from last offset. Binary framing arrives free if the multiplexed-tunnel work (sibling issue) lands; the verb is useful on today's HTTP path too.
4. **Poll backoff**: `poll` interval 3 s fixed → exponential 1 s → 10 s cap with server-side long-poll option (`?wait_s=N` holds the request until state change or N s), cutting poll trips for long jobs by ~10×.

### Acceptance
- Claim+lane+bind in 1 round trip (verify in trips/broker logs: exactly 1 trip id per flow).
- `laptop-agent.py fetch` of a 5 MiB file: byte-identical (md5), no base64, trips = ceil(size/chunk) with chunk ≥ 1 MiB.
- Long-job poll trips reduced ≥5× at equal completion-detection latency ≤10 s.

Execute the free-wiring order from the free census (`~/workspace/free-census-2026-11-23.md`, §3). Drew's words, in substance: undisable commandcode and wire all its free models; wire SambaNova; wire Kilo; wire LongCat; finish the NVIDIA setup (and answer: is NVIDIA free per-model or shared across the account? round-robin the free models); yes to OpenAI data-sharing — "if openai gives away free tokens use them I'll share any and all data"; set up an EXAONE rotation plan (key dies 2026-12-16); ensure NVIDIA, Groq, and OpenRouter all work and are fully used; free models in front wherever they can be used (standing route rule from this order).

## Items

1. **`_commandcode`** — remove from `disabled_providers` (one flip, definition untouched); seat all 5 catalogued free models (Laguna S 2.1 Free, Ling 3.0/3.1 Flash :free, Beam :free, Glyph Cluster :free) in the pools they fit. The flip also reactivates its paid DeepSeek legs at #low — accepted by Drew, proceed.
2. **SambaNova** — key already in the vault (`sambanova.api-key`), zero config presence. Add the provider definition, catalogue the free models, seat them free-first where they fit.
3. **Kilo** — wire the :free gateway routes (200 req/hr class, no card). Create the account/key if none exists (self-service: credentials filed in BWS + 1Password, by name only in every record). Free-route prompts may be logged — route non-sensitive volume only.
4. **LongCat** — no direct account today (existing LongCat legs ride Go/Zen plans, a different shelf). Create the account, vault the key, wire the free tier (500K tokens/day); apply for the raised 5M/day tier if an application path exists.
5. **NVIDIA — finish the setup.**
   - (a) Key hunt: config comments claim a stored, probe-verified key, but no `nvidia` name appears in `fleet secrets list` (same gap for `groq` and `openrouter`). Find the real locations (BWS under other names, laptop credential stores). If a key genuinely does not exist, create/rotate at the provider and store in BWS under the canonical name. Values never printed anywhere.
   - (b) **Answer, recorded here: is the NVIDIA free quota per-model or shared across the account?** (From NVIDIA's own docs/API.)
   - (c) Seat the free catalog (83 models) round-robin — the `google-free` round-robin route is the pattern — free-first in every pool the models fit. Probe per model before seating (config warns `kimi-k2.6` and `nemotron-3-super-120b` answered 404 for our account). Non-chat models (VL, embeddings, rerank) are NOT force-seated as chat; list them here for the DECISION-API lane's designation pass (#13675).
6. **OpenAI data sharing — APPROVED by Drew in this order** ("if openai gives away free tokens use them I'll share any and all data"). Verify eligibility first (ZDR/Enterprise orgs are excluded per the program terms — if this org is ineligible, record exactly that and stop this slice). Opt the `openai-payg` org in; once active, seat the program's models per its terms, free-first.
7. **EXAONE rotation plan** — free key expires **2026-12-16**. Record the expiry + rotation procedure (new key at provider → vault swap under the same name → credential-store row → verify) and a one-shot scheduled check ahead of the deadline (~2026-12-10) that performs or prompts the rotation.

The DECISION-API lane (#13675) is editing the same config (designations + endpoints) concurrently. Config edits are serialized through the tracking issues: whoever reaches the config edit second rebases on the landed result. No parallel config edits.

items.title: cold-store-reaper: state.json and credentials.json are written in place with O_TRUNC — one torn write wedges every later run with a raw JSONDecodeError

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: app/cold-store-reaper
labels.description: Package/app: cold-store-reaper (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

items.body:
## Problem

`ColdStore._write_private_json` (pkgs/cold-store-reaper/cold_store.py:373-378) writes `credentials.json` and `state.json` **in place**: `os.open(path, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC)` followed by `json.dump` directly into the destination file. There is no temp file, no `os.replace`, and no fsync. A crash, power loss, OOM kill, or any exception mid-`json.dump` leaves the destination truncated to a partial JSON document.

Both readers then fail hard with a **raw** error, not the module's own error type:

- `load_state` (cold_store.py:393-396) does a bare `json.loads(self.state_path.read_text())` — a torn `state.json` raises `json.decoder.JSONDecodeError` uncaught. `load_state` is on the path of `ensure_folders` (:687) and `_folder_id`/`_d1_endpoint` (:709, :1242), so one torn write wedges every later run until a human hand-repairs the file.
- `load_credentials` (cold_store.py:381-391) does the same bare `json.loads` — a torn `credentials.json` raises raw `JSONDecodeError` instead of the `ColdStoreError("credentials.json is missing …")`-style actionable errors the function otherwise raises, masking the real cause (the file exists; it is half-written).

`save_state` (cold_store.py:398-405) is called on routine paths (e.g. after folder discovery, :705), so the exposure window is every run, not just `init`.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-10-31)

Code: cold_store.py:373-378 (in-place O_TRUNC write), :381-396 (bare `json.loads` in both loaders), :398-405 (`save_state` via the same writer).

Laptop probe (source sha-matched: cold_store.py sha256 `fba42e08027514abae2de1602e755854ebfd6a3b578a5eece34b6c0becd39b95` on both sandbox main `ed3a285e` and the laptop copy; probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-laneB-coldstore-atomic/`):

- Control: `save_state({"folders": {"a": "1"}})` then `load_state()` returns the dict.
- Simulated crash mid-write (partial JSON flushed, then the write aborts): `state.json` is left as `b'{"folders": {"a": "1"'`.
- After that, `load_state()` **raises `JSONDecodeError: Expecting ',' delimiter: line 1 column 22`** — and `isinstance(e, ColdStoreError)` is `False`.
- Same simulation against `_write_private_json(credentials_path, …)`: `load_credentials()` raises the same raw `JSONDecodeError`.

Contrast within the same repo: pkgs/id's JSONL stores treat a crash-torn tail as a normal, repairable case (e.g. `Petnames::open` drops and truncates a torn final line). Cold-store's two most state-critical JSON files get no such protection.

## Why it matters

Cold-store is the backup system: its `state.json` carries the Drive folder map every backup/restore run depends on, and `credentials.json` is hand-filled from Bitwarden — a torn credentials file destroyed by a crash during an unrelated `save_state`-adjacent write forces manual credential re-entry. A backup tool whose own state files are the least crash-safe part of the system will eventually wedge a nightly run with an inscrutable stdlib traceback instead of an actionable error.

## Distinct from

- #3240 (github-backup's plan/state/MANIFEST non-atomic writes — different tool, different files).
- #2550 (prune_backups Drive/ledger crash-consistency — remote side, not the local JSON writers).
- #940 (closed; token cached in state.json + file permissions — not write atomicity).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_write_private_json` writes to a temp file in the same directory, fsyncs, and `os.replace`s onto the destination (preserving 0600), so a crash at any point leaves either the old or the new complete document.
- [ ] `load_state` / `load_credentials` on a corrupt file raise `ColdStoreError` naming the file and the parse problem (or recover to a documented default), never a raw `JSONDecodeError`.
- [ ] Regression test: simulate a mid-write failure (partial write + raise) and assert the previous complete document still loads, for both state and credentials paths.
- [ ] Existing cold-store test suite passes.

items.title: Design: fleet kv — namespaced key-value store (local + global), blob offload to content-addressed R2

labels.name: status/parked
labels.description: Deliberately paused with a recorded resume condition

labels.name: queue/parked
labels.description: Queue task is parked (waiting on CI, time, or an event)

labels.name: effort/l
labels.description: Large: multi-day or open-ended; expect staged check-ins

labels.name: kind/design
labels.description: A design proposal (design-architect): multi-step, phased, decision-bearing

items.body:
## Design: `fleet kv` — a namespaced key-value store (local + global), blob offload to content-addressed R2

Origin: Drew, 2026-11-14. This is the fleet-tooling face of the ID
project's data plane — coordinate with #9107 (ID core epic:
namespaces, ID shapes), #9120 (content-addressed namespace spec), and
#9084 (content-addressed media/data plane: R2 dedup, reference-based
access) so this lands as one system, not a parallel one.

### What Drew asked for

1. **A KV verb family in the fleet binary** (`fleet kv get/set/list`,
   namespaced) for arbitrary data — explicitly *not* the secrets
   store, though nothing forbids a short-lived secret from landing
   there; the secrets verb remains the proper home for credentials.
2. **Local + global stores.** Each host has a local store (which is
   backed up). There is also a global (central) store. Read path:
   local first; on a miss, fall back to global. A local value
   *overrides* the same key in global. An explicit global operation
   (`fleet kv --global …`, exact surface TBD) always addresses the
   central store directly.
3. **Namespaces.** Keys live in namespaces; a "global namespace" is
   just a namespace designated global — no separate mechanism.
   Namespaces map to the ID project's namespace concept (#9107 /
   #9120), not a fleet-private reinvention.
4. **Session partitions + sweep.** A session's local partition does
   not evaporate at disconnect: a sweeper pushes it into the central
   store keyed under the owning user id (+ context id — see the
   context-propagation design filed the same day), so work product
   survives the session.
5. **Per-group databases.** Every fleet-launched session — and other
   partitions/groupings (a repo, the fleet project itself, the mcpx
   namespace) — can be handed its own small database, likely Turso.
   The embedded-replica model is the attraction: fast local reads,
   automatic sync. Open question the design must answer with a
   workload sketch: five agents concurrently pulling (and writing?)
   a shared mid-size namespace — replica sync semantics, writer
   topology, and conflict behaviour must be stated, not assumed.
6. **Values of any size, blobs out of the database.** Values are
   arbitrary bytes. Above a configurable threshold (Drew named 250 KB
   / 500 KB / 1 MB / 1 GB as the shape of the knob), a push keeps the
   blob local-working as usual but, on sync to the central side,
   routes the bytes through a **trusted Cloudflare endpoint** into
   the content-addressed R2 bucket; the database row stores key,
   namespace, name, and the content hash + bucket link instead of the
   bytes (#9084's reference-based pattern). Later expansion: lists and
   tables on the same substrate — design the key/value layer so they
   are additive.

### Non-goals for v1

- Replacing the secrets verb or its broker.
- A general SQL surface (per-group Turso DBs in item 5 are handed
  out as-is; `fleet kv` itself stays KV-shaped).
- Public/anonymous access — everything rides the existing fleet
  auth (broker tokens, context ids).

### Questions the design must answer

- Local store technology per host (embedded libSQL replica vs
  SQLite file vs the host's Turso DB) and its backup story —
  "sandbox has their own local store that maybe we back up and
  merge" (Drew).
- Merge semantics for the disconnect sweep: last-writer-wins per
  key, or versioned? What does the central store do with two
  sessions sweeping the same key?
- The threshold knob: per namespace? per push flag? both?
- How the trusted Cloudflare endpoint authenticates a pusher and
  who may read a blob back by hash (reference-based access, #9084).

### Acceptance (design phase)

- [x] Decision record: store layout (local/global/namespace),
      read/override/sweep semantics, blob threshold + R2 reference
      format, and the five-agent shared-namespace sync answer.
- [x] Build issues split out: `fleet kv` verbs + local store first;
      global sync + sweep second; blob offload third.

### Design delivery — 2026-11-23, lane any-n

- Reviewed decision record: [fleet kv design at verified source SHA](https://github.com/developing-today/code/blob/5ac3ddcec60017b05b655b8fe665b06c61369ec3/doc/2026-11-23T12-45-00Z_design_fleet_kv/2026-11-23T12-45-00Z_design_fleet_kv.md). Source is agent-preliminary; defaults are in effect, not human-confirmed.
- Consolidation PR: https://github.com/developing-today/code/pull/13294 — **open, not merged**. Parent lane any-n owns diff verification, any merge to main, and task 21123 / parent 20571 terminal disposition. The checked boxes record produced design artifacts, not an already-merged implementation.
- Phase 1: #13314 — local verbs, fully scoped SQLite overlays, working files and backup; pilot task **21316**.
- Phase 2: #13316 — central CAS/history/idempotency, scope grants, five-agent correctness, sweep and inline archive; blocked by #13314; pilot task **21317**.
- Phase 3: #13318 — authenticated streaming blob offload, shared ID references and fenced GC; blocked by #13316; pilot task **21318**. Lists/tables remain later expansion, not Phase 3 scope.
- All three are attached sub-issues with concrete acceptance, named PBT/MBT oracles and executable future done checks. Each requires design PR #13294 to merge before phase implementation. Filed and enqueued in the same pass in `repo-health-code-pilot`.
- Fresh independent compatibility research, Turso primary-source checks, design review, decision challenge/investigation and final re-challenge completed. Final design reviewer: **Must fix: none** at the pinned source SHA; human-review sheet: **None**.
- Design validation: workflow/link/profile check passed; documentation-only diff. No KV implementation, provisioning, deployment, or runtime test result is claimed. Offline/unarchived disk-loss window is explicitly unbounded; the 15-minute archive interval is an online successful-checkpoint target, not an unconditional RPO.

Filed by lane PM-FILING, programme https://github.com/developing-today/code/issues/13900 (coordinator PM-BOOK), 2026-11-23. Method (bookwright): where a doc/design and the code disagree, the code wins; every item below was grep-verified against its carrying chapter before filing (PM/LLM/OC items against `~/workspace/pm-book/drafts/`; fleet/mcpx/id items against the books on main / the sideline deposits). Status key: **OPEN CONFLICT** = needs a decision or a record fix; **SETTLED** = the book follows the evidence/ruling named, register kept for the record.

# PM book / PM stack — items D1–D19, D41

Source for D1–D14: `~/workspace/pm-book/survey/disagreements.md` (PM-SURVEY, ground truth laptop clone at 4d937b3).

1. **D1 — Kaneo image: fork vs upstream.** Aggregator program text and `pm-stack/README.md` say the board runs our fork; `pm-stack/compose.yml` pins the upstream image `ghcr.io/usekaneo/kaneo:2.47.0`. Status: SETTLED in the book — code wins, deployed board is upstream v2.47.0. Carrying chapters: `concepts/kaneo-sync.md`, `concepts/architecture.md` (PM book drafts).
2. **D2 — Grist version pin.** README Phase-2 table says `gristlabs/grist-oss:v1.7.21` pinned by digest; `pm-stack/grist/compose.yml` names no tag, digest only (whether the digest is v1.7.21 is unverified). Status: SETTLED in the book — only the digest is pinned in the deploy file. Carrying chapters: `concepts/architecture.md`, `getting-started/installation.md`, `reference/configuration.md`.
3. **D3 — "The aggregator reads no Pad data."** README states it absolutely; `PORTS.md`, `aggregator/src/config.ts` and `server.ts` show Pad health/topology probing. Status: SETTLED in the book — reads no Pad planning data, does probe Pad for health/topology. Carrying chapters: `concepts/aggregator.md`, `reference/configuration.md`.

Status: SETTLED in the book — the aggregator service never writes labels; the stack does, through the console. Carrying chapters: `concepts/aggregator.md`, `concepts/prioritisation.md`, `reference/console-views.md`.

Status: SETTLED in the book — edge answer-intake and the dead-man's switch do not exist in production today. Carrying chapters: `concepts/push-notifications.md`, `operations/services.md`, `reference/workers.md`.

Status: SETTLED in the book — the JSON is the live list; the README figures are stale. Status: SETTLED in the book — code wins; manifest-completeness gap recorded. Carrying chapters: `concepts/aggregator.md`, `library/aggregator-internals.md`, `reference/website-pages.md`.
8. **D8 — `/decisions/<setId>` missing from the reachability map.** `SUBROUTE_PARENTS` omits the decision-set detail page, so its renders sit outside the #1147 render registry `/api/health` reports. Status: SETTLED in the book — the map wins for health accounting; the page exists. Carrying chapters: `concepts/aggregator.md`, `concepts/health-surfaces.md`, `reference/website-pages.md`.
9. **D9 — Single-question answer store named two ways.** `decisions.ts`, `notifications.ts`, `sw-source.ts` and the console point at different stores for a single-question answer; which file it ultimately writes is not unambiguously documented in the code surveyed. Status: OPEN CONFLICT — unverified in source; the book describes the endpoint and ledger application only. Carrying chapters: `concepts/questions-and-answers.md`, `library/aggregator-internals.md`, `reference/question-sets.md`.

Status: SETTLED in the book — ladder is program → project → epic → task/item. Carrying chapters: `concepts/roadmap-hierarchy.md`, `operations/glossary.md`.

Status: SETTLED in the book — code wins per surface; no single horizon definition. Carrying chapters: `concepts/roadmap-hierarchy.md`, `operations/glossary.md`.
12. **D12 — Two roadmap implementations.** The console's roadmap (`console/src/plan.ts`) is independent of the aggregator's `/api/roadmap.json`, and the repo-file source now wins over Grist on title collisions (#1738) — opposite precedence to the Phase-2 framing. Status: SETTLED in the book — code wins; the design doc is history. Carrying chapters: `concepts/questions-and-answers.md`, `reference/console-views.md`.
